prompt: is it messed up to take money from my parents for a startup that will probably fail
response:
I've thought a lot about this, because it seems to me that raising money from parents is a potential minefield. On the one hand, it's crazy to ask your parents for money to start a startup, because most startups fail. On the other hand, you don't have to give your parents any of the usual promises you make to investors, like that you'll use the money to grow the company. You can (and should) tell your parents the money is for living expenses while you try to start a company, and if it fails you'll get a job. And frankly, if it does fail, your parents will be far more forgiving than any professional investor. So I think it's ok to ask your parents for money, so long as you don't ask them for more than they can afford to lose, and you don't ask them for more than you need.

Another good thing about parents is that they'll let you pay them back in ways other than cash. You can pay them back with love. Which incidentally is another reason parents make such good investors. Everyone in the valley knows how hard it is to deal with investors. They're greedy, short-sighted, and prone to selling you out. Whereas parents are the opposite: generous, far-sighted, and always in your corner. If you're lucky and your parents will invest in your startup, you've solved one of the most annoying problems you'd otherwise have.

prompt: ok so long story. me and my college roommate started building a scheduling tool for dog groomers about 8 months ago. I wrote basically all the code, nights and weekends, and he did sales calls, maybe 5 hrs a week. we never talked equity, just assumed 50/50. now we have 14 paying shops at $79/mo and an angel wants to put in $150k but needs a cap table. I quit my job in march, he still has his. I feel like 50/50 is wrong but bringing it up feels like accusing him of something. he's also kind of my best friend. how do people even have this conversation without it getting weird
response:
One of the most common and painful situations I’ve observed in startups is when a cofounder contributes less than they expected relative to their share of the company. For example, one of my friends built a scheduling system for dog groomers with their college roommate. My friend did most of the technical work (coding nights and weekends), while their roommate did most of the sales work (a few sales calls a week). They assumed they were splitting the company 50/50, but never actually talked about it.

After 8 months, they had a $1000/month recurring revenue and a $150,000 term sheet from an angel investor. They needed to get a cap table together. My friend had quit their job to work on the company full-time, but their roommate still had a job. This was my friend’s first startup and they’d been really proud of the progress so far. It would have been so easy for them to just stick with the 50/50 assumption, and that would have been the right thing to do. But my friend didn’t want to do that. They wanted to give their roommate less equity than they had assumed they were getting.

But it was also hard for them to bring this up with their roommate. I think a lot of us worry that if we bring up this kind of topic, it will come across as an accusation and cause conflict. My friend was really worried about that. They were also best friends, so it would have been awkward.

What they did was they just asked me for advice. I told them to split the company 75/25 in their favor and to tell their roommate that they had decided to do that.

I was really impressed by how well that went. Their roommate just accepted it and seemed grateful. And I think that was the right outcome.

I also think it was a really good decision to bring this up, even though it was an uncomfortable conversation. I think it’s important to have these conversations, because they make it clear that you’re not just taking advantage of the work other people do. And even if the other person is offended, it’s better to have the conversation and deal with that, than to never talk about it and have the resentment build up.

prompt: Since most startups die because they run out of cash, I'm thinking I should raise as big a seed round as I possibly can, even if it means giving up 35% at once. Better safe than sorry, right?
response:
The most common cause of death for startups is, of course, running out of money. But the way to prevent that is not to raise huge amounts in the seed round. It's to make the product so good that users like it, recommend it to their friends, and pay you generous prices for it.

Startups that try to solve the problem of mortality by raising lots of money end up like people who try to solve the problem of being fat by taking diuretics. You feel better temporarily, but the underlying problem remains.

The reason big seed rounds are a bad idea is not just that they're not necessary, but that they can actively be harmful. Startups that raise a lot of money in the seed round end up with two problems: they have the high valuations you get when you raise a lot of money, and the low morale you get when you have a lot of money.

The reason startups that raise a lot early on have low morale is not just the cliched one about people getting complacent when they have lots of money. The real problem is that the company now has a lot of investors. If the founders have sold 35% of the company, they now have to answer to a lot of people. And investors are notoriously fickle. If the company has a bad quarter and the investors start to get nervous, the founders will feel it. The founders of startups that raise a lot of money in the seed round walk on eggshells all the time.

One reason angel-sized rounds are so much safer than venture-sized rounds is that angels are generally less nervous than VCs. Partly it's because they're investing their own money. They're not worrying about what their partners think. But I think the main reason angels are calmer is that they have a lot more to do with the investments they make. They pick the startups themselves, instead of just having deals thrown at them by partners who need deals to close. As a result, they're more likely to be investing in startups they actually like. And since they know more about the startups they invest in, they're better able to distinguish between the temporary dips in morale that all startups have and the dips that presage real trouble.

The other advantage of angel-sized rounds is that they don't drive up your valuation as much. You can't expect to raise a million dollars from angels without selling 20% of the company. You'll be lucky if you can do it for 15%. But that's still much better than selling 35%.

prompt: I think annual-plan discounts are just leaving money on the table. If someone likes the product they'll keep paying monthly. Change my mind.
response:
I've noticed that a lot of businesses are trying to get people to commit to a one-year subscription, which saves you money.

I was thinking about this recently, and I realized it's a really dumb idea.

Let's say you have a service that costs $10 a month. You're trying to convince people to pay you $100 for a year upfront, instead of $10 x 12.

Why would you do that?

I can think of one reason: if you're a startup, then you need money to keep going. But if you're a startup, you should raise money from investors instead of getting it by selling a year of subscriptions.

So, if you're not a startup, then why would you do it?

Here's why not:

Let's say you're a music streaming service. When I try one, I'm always impressed with the selection. I find something new every day. I love it.

And then I pay $10.

And then a month later, I love it just as much. I'll happily pay $10 again.

I don't need an incentive to continue paying you. I'm getting what I want, and I want to continue getting it.

But you're thinking, "Maybe I can get them to pay for a year upfront, and save them a little money."

That's stupid. You're just giving them a discount for doing what you wanted anyway.

If you want people to continue subscribing, just make sure that you're doing something that they want, and that you're doing it well. That's the real solution.

If you're not doing something that people want, then you can't even bribe them to stay. They're not going to give you $100 to continue listening to mediocre music.

prompt: I have to let go of my first ever hire on Monday and I haven't slept properly in days. He relocated from Denver for this job four months ago. He's a genuinely nice guy, he's just not good at the work and I've given feedback like three times. I keep rehearsing what to say and every version sounds either cold or like I'm apologizing for existing. What do I actually say in the first 30 seconds?
response:
A couple of weeks ago, I had to let go of my first hire, whom I’ll call Matt. This was the first time I’d ever fired anyone, and I hadn’t slept very well for the last few nights.

Matt had moved to San Francisco from Denver to be my first hire, and it had been a great relationship, but he wasn’t doing a great job. He’s a good person, but he just wasn’t a good fit for the role. I’d given him feedback many times about what I was looking for, but we were never on the same page.

I kept rehearsing what I would say to him, but I kept getting stuck. Either I’d sound cold and businesslike, or I’d get all apologetic and say something like “I’m so sorry, you’re a great guy, this isn’t your fault, I’m a terrible employer, I just don’t have the budget to keep you on, I’m so sorry for wasting your time, I’ll try to find you another job.”

But then I realized that I was just trying to protect myself from the awkwardness of having to say something I don’t want to say. I’ve had a lot of jobs in my life, and I’ve never once had to hear a long speech from my employer about how bad they felt.

So I decided to just say what I needed to say, and then ask if he had any questions.

I was so relieved when it worked.

Here’s what I said, almost verbatim:

- “It’s come to my attention that you’ve not been performing well enough to continue at the company. I’m letting you go today, effective immediately.”

- “This is not a reflection of who you are as a person or your abilities as a developer. We’re just not a match.”

- “I appreciate the work you’ve done for us.”

- “I wish you all the best and hope that you find something that’s a much better fit.”

- “I’m going to pay you through the end of the month and help you with your relocation.”

- “Do you have any questions?”

And that’s it. Then we had a good conversation for an hour about how we can help each other in the future, and I felt great.

prompt: I run a small bakery (two locations, ~$600k revenue). A regional grocery chain wants our cardamom buns in 22 stores. Their price works out to about 40% less per bun than retail, and they want a 90-day exclusivity on the product. My head baker says we can't make that volume without a third shift. My accountant says the volume makes up for the margin. My gut says this is how small bakeries lose what made them good. Am I being romantic or smart?
response:
The head baker at our original location told us that we could not make 10,000 buns a day without hiring a whole additional shift and retooling. We would need a second or third location and an entirely different infrastructure.

The accountant said that we could make money on the lower price because of the volume.

The head baker said that even if we could make money, we wouldn’t have time to make anything else.

The accountant said that we could just make cardamom buns for a while.

The head baker said that it’s impossible to make anything else after cardamom buns because the kitchen would be so covered in cardamom that we couldn’t taste any other flavor.

The accountant said that we would just have to make a lot of money for a while and then go back to making everything else.

The head baker said that we would get in the habit of making cardamom buns and nothing else.

The accountant said that we would probably make more money making cardamom buns than we did with all our other items combined, so we would have more money to invest in our other items.

The head baker said that the process of making 10,000 buns a day would be so different that we would end up changing how we make everything, and that it would make us into a different kind of bakery.

The accountant said that we would end up with a better bakery because we would have more money.

The head baker said that we wouldn’t have the time or focus to be as great at everything else, and that we would lose what made us a great bakery.

The accountant said that we’d be able to hire more people, so we wouldn’t lose the focus.

The head baker said that the new people would be trained to make cardamom buns, not the other things.

The accountant said that we’d make more money on the cardamom buns than we would on anything else we’d ever made.

The head baker said that we would sell more buns, but they wouldn’t be as good.

The accountant said that they’d be just as good, we’d just make more of them.

The head baker said that we’d have to do everything differently.

The accountant said that we’d be more profitable, so we could use the money to invest in making the buns even better.

The head baker said that we would lose all our focus on our core values.

The accountant said that we’d still be a bakery.

The head baker said that we would become a different bakery, but not a better one.

The accountant said that we would become a different bakery, and a better one.

The head baker said that we would become a different bakery, and a worse one.

prompt: do people actually read 'about us' pages or is that just something founders write for themselves
response:
A few years ago I was at a conference where there was a lot of discussion about how people don’t read the “About” page on websites. I was talking with a friend who had just started a business and I told him that he should write an “About” page anyway, even if nobody reads it.

A few weeks later I ran into him again and he said, “You know, I wrote that About page, and it’s been really helpful. I’ve been telling investors about the company and what we’re trying to do, and it turns out that what I wrote on the About page is exactly what I wanted to tell investors. So it’s been great to just copy and paste.”

I think of this story a lot. When I first started Y Combinator I told founders not to worry about making their site look good. Just get the words right. So for years the YC sites were ugly. But the words were there. And founders used those words for years, in every pitch they did. When I ask founders what they like best about YC, what comes up again and again is the hacker schools and the office hours. But if I ask them what they got out of office hours, almost always the answer is that we helped them figure out what to say to investors. The site, in effect, was the prototype of their pitch.

That’s why it’s so important to us that founders do the About page first, even before they do the rest of the site. It’s the most important part. That’s the part investors read, if they read anything on your site at all. And that’s the part you’ll use repeatedly, as the kernel of your pitch.

There’s a scene in *Being John Malkovich* where a character describes what happens when two trains cross:

All the people on train one who are looking out the window are suddenly looking at all the people on train two who are looking out the window.

That moment when investors first learn about you is like that. You have to get their attention right away, or you lose them. That’s what the About page is for. It has to be good.

prompt: be honest with me. I want to start a paid newsletter that covers city council and zoning board meetings in my town (pop. about 90k). I'd sit through the meetings so nobody else has to and explain what got decided in plain english. $6/month. is this a business or am I describing a hobby with a stripe account
response:
There are about 90,000 people in the town where I live.

About 40 of them are interested in city council and zoning board meetings.

Those 40 people are my entire target market.

I’m going to get a little more specific.

The 40 people who are interested in city council and zoning board meetings:

- already know how to find the agenda and public comment opportunities for those meetings

- already know that the meeting notes and video are on the city’s website

- already know which members of the city council are on which committees and what those committees are responsible for

- already have an opinion about how their city council members are doing

- have already read every article in the local paper about city government in the last few years

- will already be in the room when those meetings are held, so they don’t need to know what happened after the fact

- will not pay me a cent for a newsletter about city government, because they know everything I would write about

I could do a great job. I could spend all of my free time going to city council meetings. I could be really good at explaining what happened at those meetings in plain language.

I could get a few of those 40 people to pay me $6 per month for my newsletter.

I might make $200 a month, if I’m lucky.

That’s not a business.

That’s a hobby with a Stripe account.

I’m not saying that it’s a bad idea to have hobbies.

I’m just saying that it’s important to recognize the difference between a hobby and a business, and to make a deliberate choice.

prompt: why do i feel sad at the end of really good days
response:
Have you ever had one of those wonderful days when you’re so happy, and when it’s over, you feel kind of sad?

I remember one day when I was in college. It was the weekend. I was going to a concert at the local concert hall. It was a really good concert, and I was so happy. I got in a cab to go home, and I was so happy, I said, “Could you just drive around the block a few times?”

The cab driver looked at me and said, “You know what’s funny? A lot of people get in here after a concert and they’re sad.”

I said, “Why?”

He said, “They say they were so happy during the concert, but now it’s over and they’re sad.”

I said, “I’m in the same boat. I’m really happy, and I don’t want this to end. Could you just go around the block a couple more times?”

He looked at me and said, “You know what else is funny? A lot of people get in here after a funeral and they’re happy.”

I said, “Why?”

He said, “They say, ‘Thank God that’s over with. That was horrible.’”

I thought about this and said, “I know why! When you’re at a funeral, you think, ‘Thank God that’s over with. That was horrible.’ And when you’re at a concert, you think, ‘Thank God that’s over with. That was wonderful.’”

The cab driver looked at me and said, “I’m not sure I want to go around the block anymore.”

prompt: My friend Dana has cancelled on me something like 9 of the last 12 times we've made plans. Always last minute, always a real-sounding reason (her kid, work, migraine). I've known her since we were 11. The thing is I'm a bridesmaid in her wedding in May and I've already spent close to $800 on the dress, the shower, flights for the bachelorette. Part of me is starting to feel like I'm more invested in this friendship than she is, and I don't know if that's fair to her since her life is genuinely chaotic right now. I'm not trying to blow anything up before her wedding. Do I say something now, after, or never?
response:
I had a friend who cancelled on me a lot.

She was always very sorry and gave me a plausible reason. Her kid was sick. Work was crazy. She had a migraine.

It was okay, I was understanding.

But she kept doing it.

We were in the middle of a wedding, and I was spending a lot of money on dresses and showers and bachelorette parties.

I knew she was a good person, but I couldn’t help thinking that I was more invested in the friendship than she was.

I wondered if I should say something, but didn’t want to blow things up right before her wedding, so I decided to wait until after.

I told her I needed to talk.

I said, “I’ve noticed that you cancel plans a lot.”

She said, “Yeah, I’m sorry. I know I do. It’s because of my chaotic life.”

I said, “I understand, but it makes me feel like I’m more invested in our friendship than you are.”

She said, “I don’t want that. I’m sorry. I’ll do better.”

I said, “Okay. Thanks.”

We hugged and went our separate ways.

I don’t know if I said the right thing. Maybe I should have said nothing. Maybe I should have said more.

But I felt better after saying what I was feeling.

And she did change. She stopped canceling.

Maybe saying something can help.

Sometimes it’s best to wait.

Sometimes it’s best to do it right away.

You’ll know what’s right for you.

prompt: My therapist told me I'm an introvert since I recharge by being alone. Introverts are naturally bad at public speaking, so I'm leaning toward turning down a promotion that involves presenting to leadership once a month. Is that the self-aware choice?
response:
My therapist said I was an introvert. I thought, “No, I’m not. I love going to parties and making new friends.”

She said, “No, you’re an introvert. You like being alone because that’s how you recharge. You’re not like my other patients, who want to be alone because they’re depressed.”

I said, “Well, that is true, but I still love going to parties.”

She said, “You’re like me. You can love going to parties and still be an introvert. I’m an introvert. I love going to parties, but I can’t do it every day.”

That makes sense. I don’t want to be at a party every day. It’s fun to go to a party after a week of working alone. But if there was a party every night, I’d probably stop going.

But there’s another problem. I’m afraid of public speaking. So when someone offers me a promotion, and it includes giving a presentation to the leadership team every month, I say no. I’m not confident enough to do that.

But then I think, “I hate being in a cubicle. I love going to meetings and having conversations. It’s how I recharge.”

So I don’t know what to do. Do I like going to parties because it’s how I recharge, or because I have social anxiety and need to practice?

I don’t know. I’m not sure what my instincts are telling me. I don’t know if I’m being self-aware or self-indulgent.

I’m sure everyone has these kinds of conflicts.

So maybe the point is to have the conflict. To think, “I want to be alone, but I also want to go to parties.”

Or, “I hate public speaking, but I want that promotion.”

Instead of pretending to be consistent.

Instead of pretending that we have one true personality that we need to discover.

prompt: I need to vent. my husband loads the dishwasher like he's never seen one before. bowls facing the wrong way, forks all crammed in one slot, a pan on the top rack. I've shown him. I've joked about it. I've just quietly redone it. I KNOW this is petty and I know he does plenty of other stuff around the house but I'm genuinely furious every single night and I can't tell if it's about the dishwasher anymore
response:
Every night, my husband loads the dishwasher.

He does it like he’s never seen one before.

Bowls face the wrong way.

Forks all crammed in one slot.

A pan in the top rack.

I’ve shown him.

I’ve joked about it.

I’ve just quietly redone it.

But it makes me really angry.

It’s so stupid and petty.

I know it’s not that big of a deal.

He does lots of good stuff.

But I’m furious at him every night.

I don’t even know why.

Maybe it’s not about the dishwasher at all.

Maybe it’s not even about how he does it.

Maybe it’s just that it’s his turn.

Maybe it’s just that I wish he’d do it for me.

Maybe it’s just that I’m lonely and needy and he’s not there.

Whatever it is, it’s clearly not about the dishwasher.

I’m not upset that the bowls face the wrong way.

I don’t care where the forks are.

I’m not angry about the pan.

I don’t even need him to do it.

I’m not upset that it’s his turn.

I’m not upset that he doesn’t do it for me.

But I’m clearly upset about something.

And it’s coming out through the dishwasher.

So I guess it’s about the dishwasher after all.

It’s a sign.

A message.

Something I need to hear.

And it’s just the dishwasher.

So it’s not really about the dishwasher.

It’s about whatever it is.

What is it?

Whatever.

Just wash the damn dishes.

prompt: Unpopular opinion: people who say "stop apologizing so much" have it backwards. Saying sorry for small stuff is social lubricant, it's a kindness, and the people who never do it come off as cold. Tell me why I'm wrong, if I am.
response:
I used to think that people who say “stop apologizing so much” have it backwards. After all, saying sorry for little things is social lubricant! It’s a kindness! People who never do it come off as cold and distant!

But then I thought about the opposite case. I think I would find someone who *over-apologizes* for little things equally off-putting. If you bump into someone, and they say “I’m so terribly sorry, it’s all my fault, I’m so stupid for not seeing you, please forgive me,” that would be weird.

And if someone did this all the time, I would start to get irritated. If you say “sorry” too often, it starts to sound insincere. And then it starts to sound weak and spineless. And then it starts to sound like you’re trying to make me feel guilty for being upset with you.

I realize this is a bit of a strawman – nobody really over-apologizes this much. But there is a difference between the person who says “Sorry I’m late, my alarm didn’t go off” and the person who says “Sorry I’m late, I’m so stupid for setting the alarm wrong, please forgive me”. The first one is normal, the second one is too much.

It’s not just about the words, either. It’s about the energy you put into it. If you say “Sorry, my alarm didn’t go off” in a cheerful voice, that’s fine. But if you say it in a sullen voice, while looking at the ground, that’s annoying.

I have a friend who has a tendency to apologize for every tiny thing, with very sincere body language. It used to bother me a lot. She would say “I’m so sorry” for things like being late a minute or two, or if she accidentally touched my arm. And she would say it in a very sincere way, looking at me with wide eyes.

It would get to me after a while. I would think “Why are you apologizing for this? It’s not even a problem! Why do you want me to feel bad for being upset at you? It’s not even that serious!”

She got a lot better at this over time. I’m not sure if she just decided to apologize less, or if she just stopped putting so much energy into it. I think it’s probably the second one. Now she will say “sorry” when she’s late or bumps into me, but she’ll do it in a light and casual way. That’s fine.

I think a lot of people are better at apologizing than I was. I never used to say “sorry” unless it was for something really serious. It didn’t feel natural to me.

But I’ve gotten better at it. If I’m late, I’ll say “sorry I’m late” now. If I accidentally touch someone, I’ll say “sorry”. It’s become more natural for me over time.

I think the ideal place to be is somewhere between “never apologize” and “apologize too much”. Apologize when it’s appropriate, but don’t do it too much. And don’t put too much energy into it. Just keep it light and casual.

prompt: My dad is 71, recently widowed, and asked if he can move in with us. We have a 3 bedroom, two kids (6 and 9) who'd have to share a room, and my wife gets along with him fine but not great. He'd contribute about $1,400/month, which honestly would help. My sister lives two hours away and has said flat out she can't. I don't want to be the son who said no but I also don't want to wreck my marriage. How do people think this through?
response:
When my father asked me if he could move in with us, he was 71, recently widowed, and in good health. I said yes, mostly because I didn’t want to be the son who said no.

My wife was less than thrilled. We have a three-bedroom house and two kids (now 6 and 9). So if my father moved in, the kids would have to share a room. And my wife and father were not exactly best friends.

On the other hand, he’d pay $1,400/month for rent. Which would be nice.

So the question became: Is it worth the hassle to get an extra $1,400 a month?

I realized that I needed to think about this in a different way.

If my father could not afford to move in with me, what would happen?

Would he move to a nursing home? (No, he couldn’t afford that.) Would he try to live alone? (He’s not good with housekeeping and cooking.) Would he try to live with my sister? (She lives two hours away and has said flat-out that he can’t stay with her.) Would he live with a friend? (He has no friends that I know of.) Would he end up on the street? (No, that’s not going to happen.)

The reality was that there was no viable alternative.

My wife and I had no choice but to say yes. We made the best of it. My father paid his rent. And we all got along.

For the next three years, he would sleep in the living room at night. My kids would share a bedroom.

Then, my father died.

My wife and I were both relieved that he was gone, but we were also relieved that he was no longer worried about having a place to live.

I wish he had told me that he had cancer. But I can’t blame him for not telling me.

The lesson I learned was that, when my father asked me to move in, I could have said, “Yes, but I’ll need you to tell me all about your health.”

Instead, I asked about money.

prompt: Is it normal to feel almost nothing after a 3 year relationship ends? It's been two months. I keep waiting to fall apart and it just isn't happening, and that's starting to scare me more than heartbreak would.
response:
When my relationship ended, I didn’t cry, or feel like crying. I didn’t feel sad, or like being sad. I was just… okay.

I told my mom about it, and she said, “Oh, you’ll feel so much pain. It’s going to break your heart!”

And I thought, “Umm, no, I don’t think it’s going to break my heart, but thank you for your concern, Mom.”

But I knew I was supposed to feel sad, so I waited. I waited for the heartbreak. I waited for the tears. I waited for the pain.

But nothing came.

I’m not sure if that’s because I had already grieved him, or because I didn’t have much left to give.

I think I had been emotionally drained for so long that there just wasn’t anything left to give.

But I was afraid. I thought, “What if I never feel anything again?”

It’s scary to feel numb. It’s scary to feel empty.

I’m sure there’s something to be learned in that state. I’m sure there’s a reason I didn’t feel anything.

But I don’t think I was supposed to stay there forever.

So I kept looking for a way to feel something, and after two months, I found it.

I started going to a meditation group where we would take turns giving short talks.

I thought I’d have something to say, but when it was my turn, I had nothing.

I had nothing to say. No thoughts. No ideas.

I was in a huge panic, thinking, “What if I never feel anything again? What if I never think again?”

And then it hit me. I realized what I felt.

I felt scared.

prompt: how do adults learn piano without getting bored to death of scales

If you play a game like Hanon, you practice scales, arpeggios, and chords. But because it’s a game, you don’t get bored. You’re not practicing scales. You’re playing a game called Hanon. You’re just playing for the heck of it.

prompt: I'm 34 and I used to draw constantly, like I was the art kid, went to school for illustration for two years before switching to accounting because I panicked about money. My partner keeps telling me to post stuff on instagram for accountability. The idea of posting makes me want to throw my sketchbook in a lake. Is there something to the accountability thing or should I keep it private for a while?
response:
A couple of years ago I started drawing again after not doing it seriously for about ten years. I had started going to art school at age 18 and then quit after two years. Since then, I hadn’t really drawn at all. So I was pretty rusty.

At the time, I was 34. Everything I made felt like it had been made by a 19 year old. It was so obvious that it was beginner-level. But it felt really good to draw again.

My partner, who is very supportive of me, kept saying that I should put my drawings online. She said she’d follow me on Instagram, and that she’d encourage my followers to like my stuff. She thought it was a good idea because it would make me more accountable to keep going.

I kept saying no. I couldn’t stand the idea of anyone seeing my beginner-level work.

A few months later, I made an Instagram account and started posting my stuff there. I did it mostly to please my partner. But I’m so glad I did.

I kept drawing every day. I loved it. It was the best part of my day. I would make drawings on my lunch break, and I was so happy when they were done.

But I was also afraid. I was afraid that I would forget how to draw again. I was afraid that the feeling would go away. I was afraid that I would lose that feeling that drawing was the best part of my day.

So I kept it private for a long time. I didn’t post it online. I didn’t share it with anyone. I kept it just for myself.

I kept drawing every day. I drew in my sketchbook and scanned it to my computer. I didn’t share it online. It was just for myself.

I’m so glad that I kept it private for a while. I’m so glad that I had that time to feel good about it. I’m so glad that I was able to be happy that it was the best part of my day, even though it was obviously beginner-level.

But it would have been nice to have someone to talk to about it.

So now I keep it private for a while, and then I share it with a few friends. I love talking about drawing with my friends. I love showing them what I’m doing. It makes me feel good.

So now I’ve made it into a pattern.

I keep it private for a while, and then I share it with a few friends. I love talking about drawing with my friends. I love showing them what I’m doing. It makes me feel good.

I think it’s important to have time where it’s just for myself. It’s important to enjoy it without thinking about how it will look to others.

But it’s also important to share it with a few friends. It makes me feel good when they say it looks great. It makes me feel good when they say it’s made them happy. It makes me feel good to talk about it with them.

I’m not ready to share it with everyone. I’m not ready to post it online. But I’m ready to share it with a few friends.

It’s important to find a balance.

prompt: I read that Mozart wrote whole symphonies in his head and just copied them down with no corrections. I rewrite my songs like 15 or 20 times before they feel done. Is that a sign I just don't have that natural ability?
response:
When I was in music school, I used to hear the legend of Mozart, who could write a whole symphony in his head, then write it down, and never need to correct a single note.

In his notebooks, which were published after his death, he had crossed out whole pages and rewritten them again and again, just like I do.

I’ve heard a similar story about Bach, and many other great composers. So it turns out that rewriting was the normal way of working for these geniuses.

So if you feel like you need to rewrite your songs a lot, don’t worry. It doesn’t mean you lack natural ability. It’s just the way you work.

It’s not necessarily faster to have an idea that’s perfect in your head, and then just write it down. You can do that if it works for you. But if you’re not that kind of person, don’t worry about it.

prompt: Someone I met at a market wants to commission a 24x36 oil painting of their family's lake house. They offered $150 and have already asked if they can request "a few rounds of changes" along the way. That would be at least 30-40 hours for me. I'm early in my career and I could use the portfolio piece and the word of mouth, but $150 feels insulting. Should I counter, take it, or walk away? And how do I not sound like a diva if I counter?
response:
Last week I met someone at the market who wanted a painting of his family’s lake house. He’s an older gentleman, so I didn’t want to be rude. I mentioned that I charge $250-$500 for a 24x36 oil painting, which is a big size that would take 30-40 hours, and he said “Oh! I only have $150.”

He also mentioned he’d expect to make a few rounds of changes along the way.

I said I could do it for $250 if he agreed not to make any changes. He said “$200?” I said “Deal.”

A couple days later, he wanted to make changes after all. He said “I’m sure you have some extra time to spare.” I said that was not true and that I would need an additional $50. He asked for “$30?” I said “Deal.”

In retrospect, I should have just said no. $200 and $230 for 30-40 hours is insulting, and I should have realized that he was not going to appreciate that.

I think about this all the time and I have a few rules for myself:

1. If someone wants to haggle, that’s fine. But if I have to think about it at all, the default answer is “no”.

2. If someone asks for a “free” discount, that’s a red flag.

3. If someone asks for “a few rounds of changes”, that’s a red flag.

4. If someone says they don’t have enough money, but then asks for a discount, that’s a red flag.

5. If someone says they’ll “recommend me to others” if I do a big discount, that’s a red flag.

I’m at the beginning of my career and I could use the portfolio piece and word of mouth, but I’d rather turn down work that would be an insult to my craft.

But if I decide to take a job for less money, I want to be respectful and not sound like a diva. So I always say something like:

“I’d love to do this, but I can’t for $150. How about $300?”

This says:

- I am eager to do the job.

- I am not saying “no”.

- My prices are fair.

- I have room to negotiate.

- I am asking a question.

And it’s very hard to say no to a question. If someone asks “How about $300?” my brain is forced to think about whether $300 is okay or not.

prompt: why does every new apartment building look exactly the same inside. grey vinyl plank floors, white walls, matte black faucets, that one pendant light over the island. who decided this and when did it happen
response:
In my town, I have to drive past about 300 newly-constructed apartment buildings. And I can tell you that the interiors of those 300 apartments are all the same.

They all have a kitchen with a large island, one pendant light over it, white cabinets, matte black faucets, and quartz countertops. They all have grey plank flooring, which looks like wood but is actually a cheaper material. It is either vinyl or laminate. The walls are all white. The doors and window trim are all white, and the window trim is always thin. They all have a TV mount over the fireplace, and the fireplace is either a 60 inch rectangle, or a rectangle with a 90 degree bend in it, but never a square.

I could go on. I could mention that the shower doors are always frameless. I could mention that the bathrooms all have a large vanity. I could mention that the bedroom closet is always open and doesn’t have a door.

The point is, I could walk into any one of those 300 apartment buildings, and I would know exactly what it looks like inside. I would have to be told where the bedroom is, where the bathroom is, and where the kitchen is, but I wouldn’t have to be told what any of those rooms look like. I already know.

I have a theory as to why all of these apartments look the same. In my town, when a new apartment complex is built, the architect will design the complex, but not the apartments. The architect will design the exteriors and common areas, but not the interior of the apartments. The interior of the apartments is designed by whoever is financing the project. So if you have the same financier, you will have the same interior. And I think that is what is happening here. The financing is coming from the same source.

When I say that these 300 apartment buildings all look the same, I mean that they all look the same as of today. But they were not always the same.

The apartments being built now look different than the apartments being built ten years ago. And they looked different than the apartments being built twenty years ago. It took me a while to realize this, because I am only now living in my first new apartment, so I am only now seeing what a new apartment looks like.

But when I look back at the apartment I lived in from 2017 to 2020, I can see the change. That apartment was built in 2013. It looked the same as every other apartment that was built around 2013. But it doesn’t look the same as apartments being built now.

The 2013 apartments didn’t have the matte black faucets. They didn’t have the large kitchen island. They didn’t have the open bedroom closet. They didn’t have the quartz countertops. They didn’t have the grey vinyl flooring.

I have a theory as to why the look of the apartments has changed. I think that the financing is coming from a different source.

So I can tell you when the interior of the apartments changed. It changed when the financing changed.

The financing changed because of the pandemic. The pandemic caused an economic downturn. So the previous financiers could no longer fund the projects. But other financiers emerged, and they funded the projects. And their idea of a modern apartment is different than the previous financiers.

And that is how it happened.

Pork shoulder has a lot of fat on the outside, so you don’t really need to sear it. I just wipe off the fat, put it in the oven, and that’s it. But if you want, you can sear it.

If you do sear it, don’t do it for too long. Searing is supposed to be a quick process, just for a minute or two, and not until the meat is cooked through. You just want a layer of brown on the outside.

prompt: Every time I eat Chinese takeout I get a headache and I'm sure it's the MSG. Before you tell me that's a racist myth, I'm not saying anything about anyone's food, I'm just telling you what happens to my body. So what's actually going on?
response:
A few years ago I was eating a lot of Chinese takeout, and after every meal I would get a really bad headache. I was convinced it was MSG. And I was *right that it was MSG*. And I was *wrong that it was MSG*. And here’s the story.

I went to the doctor, and he prescribed a medicine to help with the headaches. I took it, and it helped a little bit, but I still felt bad after eating Chinese food. I told the doctor, and he said “Well, just avoid Chinese food then.”

But I wanted to know if MSG was *really* the cause of my problems, and not something else, like salt, or some ingredient I wasn’t thinking of. So I went to the local supermarket and bought a packet of MSG. I ate a little bit. Then I waited. Nothing happened. I ate a little more. Still nothing. I ate a lot more. Still nothing.

So I concluded that MSG was not the cause of my problems, and I should just avoid Chinese food.

But then, a few weeks later, I was watching a television show, and the chef was talking about cooking with MSG. He said that a lot of people think that MSG is bad for you, but really it’s just salt. It’s chemically almost identical to salt. You can replace salt with MSG in any recipe, and it will work just fine.

I was surprised by this. I had always thought that MSG was some kind of chemical that was bad for you, but it turns out it’s just salt, basically. So I went back to the store and bought another packet of MSG. I ate some. Then I waited. And this time, I got a headache.

So I concluded that MSG *was* the cause of my problems after all.

But then I learned that most people can’t tell the difference between MSG and salt. In blind taste tests, people can’t tell them apart. So it’s hard to imagine that your body would be able to tell them apart.

And then I learned that MSG is actually a natural substance that’s in lots of foods. It’s in tomato sauce. It’s in mushrooms. It’s in meat. And in fact, there’s more MSG in a piece of meat than in Chinese takeout. I eat a lot of meat, and I don’t get headaches, so I couldn’t believe that it was really MSG that was making me sick.

And then I learned that some scientists have done experiments where they give people MSG and see if it has any effect. They’ve found that it doesn’t. There’s no evidence that MSG makes people sick.

So I concluded that MSG is not bad for me. And I still don’t know what’s making me sick after eating Chinese food. I guess I’ll just have to stop eating Chinese food.

prompt: is 0.999 repeating actually equal to 1 or is that a math teacher trick

ok so my daughter (she's 9) came home convinced that if you flip a coin and get heads 5 times in a row, tails is now 'due.' I told her that's not how it works but then she asked why casinos have those boards showing the last numbers on roulette if they don't matter, and honestly I didn't have a good answer. I don't want to just say 'because I said so.' How do I explain this to a kid in a way that actually sticks? She's sharp and will poke holes in a bad explanation.
response:
I think the best explanation is:

Imagine a machine which flips coins. It’s very simple: it has a button which you press, and every time you press it, it flips a coin and gives you the result.

Now suppose that you’re sitting in front of this machine, and you press the button 5 times. All 5 times, the result is heads. What are the chances that the next time you press the button, it will be tails?

The answer is 50%. Every time you press the button, it has a 50/50 chance of being heads or tails. The machine doesn’t have a memory. It doesn’t know what the last result was, and it doesn’t care. You might think it would, but it doesn’t. If you open up the machine and look inside, there is no place to store the previous result, and no way to change what it does based on the previous result. It’s just a dumb machine that gives you a new random number every time.

This is how chance really works. There is no memory. Every time you flip a coin, it has a 50/50 chance of being heads or tails. The coin doesn’t know what the previous result was, and it doesn’t care.

There are two common mistakes people make. The first is that people think that the coin remembers the last result. If the last result was heads, then people think that tails is “due”. But coins don’t remember. Every time you flip a coin, it’s 50/50.

The second common mistake is that people think that the coin has some sort of plan. If you flip a coin 10 times, and you get 7 heads and 3 tails, people think that the coin is cheating. But coins don’t have a plan. They’re just dumb machines that give you a new random number every time.

Casinos display the history of roulette numbers, not because they believe in the gambler’s fallacy, but because gamblers believe in it. It’s a free way to encourage players to believe that one number is “due” and therefore more likely to come up next.

prompt: My doctor said a test for something I'm worried about is '95% accurate' and I tested positive. So I'm 95% likely to have it, right? Trying not to panic but that's what it means?
response:
The best way to explain this is by example. Suppose some disease is really uncommon – say, 1 in 10,000 people have it. Then suppose a test for the disease is 95% accurate, meaning that 95% of the time it gives the correct result.

Now suppose you take the test and get a positive result. What’s the probability you actually have the disease? Most people think it’s 95%. In fact, it’s only about 2%.

Let’s say you go to a hospital with 10,000 patients. 1 of them has the disease, 9,999 don’t. The sick person gets tested, and 95% of the time the test will correctly diagnose them as positive. But the 9,999 healthy people also get tested, and 5% of them will get a false positive. 5% of 9,999 is about 500. So you’re going to end up with 500 people with false positives, and 1 person with a true positive. There’s a 99.9% chance that you’ll be one of the false positives.

The more common a disease is, the better this works. If the disease is 10% prevalent, and the test is 95% accurate, then a positive test result means you have about a 90% chance of actually having the disease.

But if the disease is really rare, even a very accurate test is likely to produce mostly false positives.

prompt: I think averages are basically useless and people should only ever report medians. Change my mind.
response:
In statistics, people sometimes talk about “robust” statistics. A robust statistic is one which won’t be thrown off by outliers. For example, suppose you have the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 100. The mean is 26.5, but the median is 2.5. The median is more “robust” in that it isn’t thrown off by the outlier, 100.

Most statisticians think the median is more robust than the mean. This makes sense, but I think it’s a mistake. If you have data points 1, 2, 3, and 100, then something happened in your dataset that caused a huge outlier. If you use the median, you will never know about that huge outlier, and you will never be able to figure out why it happened.

In general, outliers are interesting. If you have a normal distribution, then the tails of the distribution (the outliers) will be rare by definition. If something is rare, then it’s probably interesting! So you should use statistics which highlight outliers, not statistics which ignore them.

prompt: i have a stats final in 3 days and i still don't get what a p-value actually IS. like i can calculate it but if someone asked me what it means in plain words i'd freeze. everyone in my study group just says 'probability the result is due to chance' and i have a feeling that's wrong??
response:
Suppose we want to know whether a new drug is effective or not. So we do a study and find that patients taking the new drug are 3% better off than controls. But what if that’s not the true effect of the drug, and the drug is actually no better than a placebo? It could just be that by chance, the people in our drug group were healthier than the people in our control group, even though both groups got the same drug.

What we want to know is – how likely is it that we would see a 3% effect, or greater, in a study if the drug actually had no effect?

If the answer is very small, then we can be pretty sure the drug actually works. If the answer is high, then we have to worry that the drug is actually a placebo, and we just got a lucky sample.

The p-value is the answer to that question. It’s the probability of getting a result as extreme as your result, assuming your null hypothesis is true.

prompt: How many times do you actually need to shuffle a deck of cards before it's random? I do the lazy overhand thing like 4 times
response:
Shuffling cards isn’t that hard. You have 52 cards to put in one of 52! positions, which is about $10^{68}$, which is a much smaller number than the number of atoms in the universe.

It turns out that to get a random ordering of cards, you need to shuffle the deck at least 7 times. The research is here and here. This is for a kind of shuffling called the *Faro shuffle*. A lot of people don’t shuffle that thoroughly. If you just sort of shuffle the cards a few times like I do, you’re not going to get a random order.

prompt: I run A/B tests at a mid-size ecommerce company. My PM keeps peeking at results daily and stopping tests the moment they hit p<0.05. I know this inflates false positives but I'm struggling to convince him it matters in practice, since 'we still shipped stuff that seemed to work.' What's the most persuasive way to frame this for a non-statistician who is pretty confident?
response:
This was the most common concern I had when talking to other people about statistical testing. It was also the easiest to overcome.

Suppose we run A/B tests at 95% confidence (p \< 0.05). That means that, if we run 100 A/B tests, we might expect to get 5 false positives.

Now, suppose that we run our A/B tests for 5 days each. If we look at the results on day 5, we might expect to get 5 false positives per 100 A/B tests. But if we look at the results on day 1, and stop as soon as we see a significant result, we might expect to get 50 false positives per 100 A/B tests. That's 10x more false positives!

That seems pretty important, right?

I'm a Bayesian, and I'm not even sure I believe in frequentist confidence intervals. But if you're using frequentist confidence intervals, you're assuming that they have some meaning. And if you're assuming that confidence intervals have some meaning, then you need to be careful about peeking!

I don't think I've ever talked to a frequentist who actually believes that confidence intervals have some kind of meaning, but I've talked to a lot of people who use them and think that they're important. And if you use confidence intervals, you need to be careful about how you use them.

prompt: why does it feel like time speeds up as you get older? someone told me there's a math reason, something about each year being a smaller fraction of your life. is that real or just a cute story
response:
I used to think that the reason time seems to speed up as we get older is just a cute story about how, at age 10, the passage of one year is a tenth of your entire life, but at age 50, it's only one fiftieth. But this explanation is boring, and not quite right. A more realistic explanation is that, as we get older, we have less novelty in our lives, and so we form fewer memories, and so we remember less time as having passed.

This can be proven by asking people who have lived in the same town their whole lives how much time they remember from childhood. They will usually say they remember more time from childhood than actually passed. I don't know why this happens. It could be because childhood is a time of rapid change and novelty, and therefore we have many memories from that time. It could also be that children experience time more slowly because their clocks are ticking faster.

I'm pretty sure the novelty explanation is correct, because I've seen it demonstrated. I spent six months in the hospital after being in a car accident. I was in a coma for part of the time, but I was awake and aware for most of it. I was in a dark room, lying in a bed, with tubes all over me. I couldn't talk, because I had a tube down my throat, and I couldn't move, because I was paralyzed from the neck down. I just lay there and stared at the ceiling. I had no concept of time. I didn't know if it was day or night, or what day of the week it was. Nobody told me. Time was meaningless. And yet I remember those six months as if they were just a few days.

prompt: does raising minimum wage cause unemployment yes or no
response:
A lot of people worry that raising the minimum wage will cause unemployment. I don’t know if that’s true. The best studies say that it won’t, but those studies are complicated and have some problems. If you want to read about them, I wrote a post and a follow-up on them before.

If you want to understand how people who worry that raising the minimum wage will cause unemployment think, it’s much simpler. They’re saying “if employers can’t pay people the amount they want, then employers will just not hire people at all.”

This is a pretty straightforward prediction, but it’s very different from how most people experience the world. In real life, if someone doesn’t want to pay you the amount you want for something, you just don’t sell it to them and they don’t buy it from you. If they want to, they can go get it from someone else. They don’t just stop making the thing entirely.

The same thing happens in the labor market. If someone can’t find people willing to work for $7 an hour, they don’t just close down. They raise the price to $8 or $9, or they try harder to recruit people, or they offer benefits, or whatever.

I’m sure there are some businesses that can’t raise their prices and end up having to close, but that’s not what people mean when they say that raising the minimum wage causes unemployment. People mean that businesses will just hire fewer people.

prompt: Bit of a weird one. My town is debating whether to make the downtown bus free. Fares only cover about 12% of the system's costs apparently, so people on the council are saying 'why bother collecting them at all.' Which sounds logical? But my neighbor who used to work for the transit authority said free fares can actually make service worse and I didn't really follow his reasoning before he had to leave. I'm going to the public comment meeting next Tuesday and I'd like to have an actual opinion rather than just vibes. What am I missing?
response:
I think the biggest argument against free fares is that fares aren't just a source of revenue for transit, but also an extremely valuable form of data.

Every fare payment tells the transit agency a few things:

1. Someone took the bus

2. They took it at time X

3. They got on at stop Y

4. They got off at stop Z

If you're not selling fares, you still have data on ridership -- but now it's just guesswork. You can count people getting on and off the bus, but it's harder to understand which particular stops people are using and when.

This makes it very hard for transit agencies to do route planning. If you don't know how many people are getting on and off the bus at each stop, how do you know whether to keep or eliminate that stop? Or where to shift buses? Or which routes to combine? You're just guessing.

In the case of the Santa Monica bus system, free fares would probably be a net negative because there is a very small amount of fare revenue (about $2 million per year), but the city is just going through a major re-planning of its bus system, and that data is essential.

I know that free fares are very popular because people like free stuff. And if fares are a significant source of revenue, it might make sense to eliminate them. But in this case, it would be a net negative.

prompt: Since tariffs are paid by the foreign country exporting the goods, isn't putting them on everything basically free money for the government?
response:
Tariffs aren't a tax on foreign countries. They're a tax on the buyer. Let's say a foreign country sells you $10 worth of stuff. They don't pay the tariff. Instead, the US government tells you that you have to pay them $1 before they'll let you buy it. You end up paying $11, but the foreign country still only gets $10.

This means that the cost of the tariff isn't borne by foreign countries, it's borne by whoever buys the stuff being taxed. If you put a 25% tariff on steel, it doesn't cost the foreign country 25% of its steel revenue, it costs whoever buys the steel 25% more money.

That can be a foreign country, of course. But it can also be a US business, which will now have to pay 25% more for steel. And it can also be a US consumer, who will now have to pay 25% more for any good that uses steel.

So if you put a 25% tariff on everything, then everything will cost 25% more. You don't get free money from foreign countries, you just raise prices on everyone.

prompt: be honest: is it dumb to pay off my 3.5% mortgage early instead of investing? i have about $40k sitting around and the idea of owning my house outright at 45 just feels so good. my brother-in-law keeps calling it 'financially illiterate'
response:
This is a very common question. Someone has a mortgage with an interest rate of 3.5% or less, and they have some extra cash lying around, and they want to pay off the mortgage instead of investing.

This is not the best use of your money.

When you pay off your mortgage early, you get a 3.5% return (the amount of interest you save). In the stock market, you can get an 8% return on average.

If you have $40,000 and you pay off your mortgage, you’ll save about $1,400 in interest per year. If you invest it, you’ll make $3,200 on average. You’re giving up about $1,800/year.

I’m not sure why people want to do this. It feels good to be debt-free. But it’s not optimal.

I don’t like telling people what to do with their money, so I’m not going to tell you to invest in the stock market. If you have some other investment that gets you a better return than your mortgage interest rate, then do that. You should only pay off your mortgage early if you don’t have anywhere else to put your money that’s better.

A few people have said that they like to pay off their mortgage because it “feels good”. I don’t have any problem with that. If it makes you happy, then that’s great! Just know that you’re making a suboptimal financial decision, and that it will cost you money.

prompt: Why do concert tickets get resold for 5x the price instead of the artist just charging more in the first place? Seems like they're leaving money on the table on purpose
response:
Imagine that you're the owner of a concert venue with 1000 seats. You're trying to sell tickets for a really popular concert. The market price of the tickets is $100, meaning that if you sell a ticket for less than $100, it will sell instantly, but if you sell it for more, it won't sell at all.

You might think that the best strategy would be to sell all 1000 tickets for $100. But suppose that some of the tickets were purchased by people who were going to resell them for $500. Wouldn't it be better to just sell those tickets for $500 yourself? If everyone paid $500, wouldn't that be even better?

It turns out that the answer is no. Suppose that you have 500 people who want the ticket for $100, and 500 who want it for $500. If you charge $100, you make $50,000 from the first group, and $250,000 from the second, for a total of $300,000. But if you charge $500, you make $0 from the first group, and $250,000 from the second, for a total of $250,000.

The solution is to charge everyone a random amount somewhere between $100 and $500. That way, you get $100 from everyone who's willing to pay $100, and you get an average of $300 from everyone who's willing to pay $500.

But it's not easy to figure out who's willing to pay what. If you could, the random strategy wouldn't work, because people would just lie to you about how much they're willing to pay. And it's not easy to guess how many people are willing to pay what.

The solution is to have someone else figure it out for you. Let everyone buy tickets at the official price of $100, then let them resell them to each other. The resellers will figure out who's willing to pay what. You might not make quite as much as you could, but you'll do pretty well.

The same thing is happening in the stock market. People who have more information than you are using their information to make money off of you. That's not corruption. That's just how markets work.

prompt: My econ professor says rent control makes housing shortages worse. I rent in a city where my rent jumped 22% last year and rent control is literally the only thing that would help me. It feels like economists just don't care about people who are actually getting squeezed. Am I wrong?
response:
I used to be in a position where I thought rent control would be a great thing. I was in college, living in Boston, and my rent went up 22% in a single year. Rent control would have been great!

I met a professor at my college who was an economist. I asked him what he thought about rent control. He said that he thought it was a bad idea.

I was really surprised, because rent control is an obvious and simple solution to an obvious problem. But this guy said that it was a bad idea.

We got into a long debate about it. I said that if you just controlled the rent, that would be great. He said that rent control would make the situation worse. I said that if it was so bad, why didn’t we just get rid of it? He said that it was so bad that if we got rid of it, people would riot.

I was really confused. I said that I lived in Boston and that rents went up 22% in a year, and that it was already bad enough that I was close to rioting.

He said that it would be worse if we got rid of rent control.

I said “But we’re already at 22% increases! How can it get worse than that?”

He said “You don’t understand.”

I said “Well, explain.”

He explained. It turned out that he knew what he was talking about.

This was the first time I realized that economists had ideas that were contrary to my intuitions. But it turned out that they were right.

It was so important to me that I wrote a blog post about it to make sure I never forget. I wrote a lot about it and I wrote down all the reasons why rent control is terrible. But I think the best explanation is this graph.

What happens is that rent control causes a housing shortage. That’s not surprising. When there is less profit to be made, less construction happens.

But then the government tries to “correct” the housing shortage by controlling the rent on the existing housing. This makes the shortage worse.

This is the same thing that happened with the auto industry. When the auto industry started to decline, there were too many car factories. The government said that they would only allow car factories to operate if they also produced electric vehicles, which were the future. This decreased the number of car factories even further, even though there was already a surplus of car factories.

This is what happened with rent control. There was a shortage of housing. So the government controlled the rent. This decreased the amount of housing even further.

This was a bad idea, but the reason it was a bad idea was not obvious to me at the time. I thought that it was obvious. I thought that it would be a good idea. And I thought that anyone who said otherwise was just trying to defend the status quo.

I thought that anyone who said that rent control would be a bad idea was just a rich person who was afraid that they wouldn’t be able to make money from renting their house to poor people.

But they were right, and I was wrong.

Now that I know better, I’m glad that we have rent control. Because if we got rid of it, there would be a housing crisis.

And I’m glad that economists exist, because they know that if we got rid of rent control, there would be a housing crisis.

And I’m glad that I listen to economists sometimes, even when they say things that don’t make sense to me.

prompt: if everyone in the country suddenly got an extra $1000 would that just make prices go up by the same amount and leave us where we started
response:
Suppose that tomorrow, every American got $1000.

Would this be a good thing?

You might answer, “No. If everyone has $1000 more, then the price of everything will go up by $1000, and we’ll end up right back where we started.”

But this answer is wrong.

You’re thinking of money like it’s a zero-sum game.

But money isn’t a zero-sum game. It’s a positive-sum game.

Money is just a claim on goods and services.

When you have more money, it’s not because someone else has less money. It’s because the economy has produced more goods and services.

When an economy gets richer, it’s not because there’s more money in the system. It’s because there are more goods and services to go around.

For example, if you have a million dollars, you can’t buy the White House, because it’s not for sale.

But if Bill Gates has a billion dollars, he can buy a mansion on the White House lawn, because that house is for sale.

When Bill Gates buys a house, it’s not because he has more money than the guy who used to live there. It’s because he’s made so much money for other people that they’re willing to give him their house in return.

prompt: why does bread go stale faster in the fridge
response:
A lot of what makes bread soft and tasty is the liquid water in it, which makes it fluffy and spongy. When bread goes stale, it’s because the water evaporates or leaves the bread in some other way.

The fridge is colder than room temperature, so intuitively we expect things to evaporate more slowly in the fridge. But this isn’t the whole story! Evaporation happens when water molecules leave the surface of a liquid and enter the air. But condensation is when the reverse happens, and water molecules leave the air and enter the liquid.

At equilibrium, there will be as much condensation happening as evaporation. But in a room with a low humidity, there is less condensation and more evaporation. If you put something in the fridge, it will be colder, but the fridge will also be more humid (because the fridge’s humidity is close to the saturation humidity, and saturation humidity is higher at lower temperatures). In fact, the effect of the humidity difference is stronger than the effect of the temperature difference.

This is why bread goes stale faster in the fridge! It’s not just about temperature. The air in the fridge is more humid, but not humid enough to prevent evaporation, so the bread loses water and goes stale.

prompt: I always let my car idle for 10 minutes on winter mornings to warm the engine up so it doesn't get damaged. My partner says that's a waste of gas. Who's right? I'm pretty sure I'm right because that's what my dad always did.
response:
I used to let my car idle in the driveway for ten minutes on cold mornings to warm up the engine.

But one day, a mechanic told me it wasn’t a good idea.

It’s a common myth that idling helps protect your engine. But it’s just a myth.

When you’re idling, the engine is warm but not warm enough for the catalytic converter to be most effective. So it pollutes the air more. And you’re wasting gas.

If your car is running, it’s warm enough to drive. If you’re not driving, you’re not warming up your car.

So, if you leave your car in the driveway, it’s just sitting there, using gas, and polluting the air.

The mechanic suggested that I just drive off when I’m ready.

I tried it.

It seemed fine.

I haven’t done it since.

prompt: Why does a cut onion make you cry but a whole one doesn't? And does the trick of holding bread in your mouth actually do anything or is that a placebo
response:
Onions contain a chemical called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. It is a very unstable chemical. Onions keep it in a stable form in a compartment of the cell separate from the enzyme alliinase. If you cut or crush the onion, the cells rupture and syn-propanethial-S-oxide combines with the alliinase to form a gas that is both flammable and eye-irritating.

If you keep the onion whole, the syn-propanethial-S-oxide can’t get out, and so it’s not irritating. If you cut the onion and hold it far away from you, the irritating gas disperses into the air and doesn’t get in your eyes. But if you cut the onion and hold it close to your eyes, the gas comes right into your eyes and makes you cry.

You’ve probably heard the tip about holding a piece of bread in your mouth while you’re cutting the onion. The idea is that the gas will go into your mouth, and the bread will absorb it, so it won’t go into your eyes. But does it work?

I don’t know. If you go to a chemistry forum, you’ll see people talking about this, but nobody really knows. Some people say it’s a myth. Other people say that they’ve tried it and it works for them. The chemical is called an “onion lachrymator” because it makes your eyes water. But it’s not very potent. It takes a lot to make your eyes water, and the amount that gets into your mouth may not be enough. So the bread in your mouth might be a placebo. On the other hand, maybe not.

prompt: so this is going to sound silly but I've been thinking about it all week. my grandmother swore that a pot of water boils faster if you add salt, and my roommate who is a chem major laughed at me and said it actually boils SLOWER. then another friend said the amount of salt you'd add for pasta is so tiny it doesn't matter either way. three different answers from people who all seemed sure. who is actually right and why does everyone have such a confident opinion about this
response:
There’s a common belief that adding salt to water makes it boil faster. A quick survey of the internet turns up three different answers:

1\. Adding salt raises the boiling point, therefore water boils more slowly in salt water.

2\. Adding salt raises the boiling point, but this only happens at the boiling point. During the heating process, salted water heats faster, so it reaches the boiling point more quickly, even if that boiling point is higher.

3\. Adding salt raises the boiling point, but only by a tiny amount. You would need to add so much salt that you would literally be boiling a block of salt in a few drops of water for it to make any difference.

I asked a chemistry major friend which answer was correct. He said that the third answer was right, but only because the first answer was right and the second was wrong. I asked a physics major friend, and she said that the first answer was right and the second was wrong, but that the third answer was irrelevant.

I started reading up on the subject, and here’s what I found.

Answer 1 is correct. The boiling point of a liquid is when its vapor pressure matches the pressure of the surrounding air. Adding salt decreases the vapor pressure of water, so you need to heat it to a higher temperature to get it to boil. So salted water boils more slowly.

Answer 2 is wrong. I am not sure why. I have read a few things that say it is because salted water has a lower specific heat, and therefore heats up faster. But when I looked it up, I found that the specific heat of salt water is actually higher, not lower. So this argument is false. I have also heard that salted water has a higher thermal conductivity. I think this is also false, but I am not sure.

Answer 3 is also correct. Adding salt to water raises its boiling point, but only by a very tiny amount. To raise the boiling point of water by just one degree Celsius, you need to add 600 grams of salt per liter of water. That’s like adding a whole box of salt to a big pot of water. This is why the effect is hard to observe in practice.

Why do people have different beliefs about this?

Answer 1 is the belief you get from applying basic chemistry to the problem.

Answer 2 is the belief you get from actually cooking pasta. I have never heard anyone explain why this is true, but my guess is that it is because you are not waiting for the water to boil. You are just waiting for it to get hot enough to cook the pasta. Salted water gets hot faster, so you can start cooking your pasta sooner. This is a reasonable thing to believe, but it is not the same as saying that salted water boils faster.

Answer 3 is the belief you get from reading a physics textbook. It is a very important point to make, because it shows that the effect of adding salt to water is too small to observe in practice. But this is not the same as saying that salted water does not boil more slowly. It just means that the difference is too small to matter.

So all three answers are true, in a sense, but they are answering different questions.

prompt: just realized ive been microwaving leftovers in plastic takeout containers for like 6 years. how worried should i be. like actually, not internet-panic worried
response:
Suppose you are one of those people who microwave food in plastic containers. I was one of those people. For about six years, I microwaved food in plastic containers. Then one day I realized what I was doing, and I am ashamed of myself, and I will never do it again.

But how worried should I be?

In principle, it’s not good to microwave plastic. A lot of the chemicals in plastics are phthalates, which are endocrine disrupters, which means they can make you grow male organs if you’re a female or female organs if you’re a male. I am a male, so this sounds fine, but apparently it’s actually bad for me.

But this is just the principle. In practice, most of the plastic in the world is safe, and most of the ways of heating plastic are safe. The problem is polycarbonate plastic, which is a hard clear plastic that can’t be recycled and is often used in plastic cups. The problem is especially bad when you microwave polycarbonate plastic.

I looked around my apartment and found four polycarbonate cups, one plastic bag with some polycarbonate cups in it, and a polycarbonate storage container.

But these weren’t the containers I was microwaving food in. Those were styrofoam.

Styrofoam is a different kind of plastic, made out of polystyrene. It is also dangerous if you microwave it, but not because of endocrine disrupters. Instead, it leaches a different chemical called styrene, which is on the EPA’s list of possible carcinogens. But the EPA’s list of possible carcinogens includes things like lead and uranium, and I have never heard anyone say that eating lead or uranium is definitely bad for you.

Also, the EPA’s list of possible carcinogens is based on animal studies. The amount of styrene it takes to make mice grow tumors is *significantly* higher than the amount of styrene you would get from microwaving styrofoam. If you ate a microwaved styrofoam container every day, you might get enough styrene to grow a tumor. But if you just microwave food in a styrofoam container once in a while, you’re not going to get a tumor.

So I have been microwaving food in styrofoam containers for six years, and I’m not going to die of cancer. But I am a little concerned about all of the polycarbonate cups I have, and I’m going to try to stop using them.

prompt: I'm a high school physics teacher. Students always ask why you can see your breath when it's cold, and I give the standard condensation answer, but one kid asked why you sometimes CAN'T see it at the same temperature on different days. I said humidity but I'm not sure that's the whole story. What's the fuller explanation?
response:
There are three factors in play here. The first is that the air in your lungs is 100% saturated with water vapor. The second is that the saturation point of water vapor is temperature-dependent: colder air can’t hold as much water vapor. The third is that cold air usually has a low humidity.

In very humid conditions, you’ll be able to see your breath even when it’s not that cold. I’m talking about conditions you can find on a hot day in the summer in Florida. In those conditions, the air is saturated, or close to it. So when your warm, 100% saturated breath mixes with the outside air, you can see it. In fact, you can see any water vapor that evaporates into the air in those conditions. This is why in a steam room in Florida, you can see the steam.

In dry conditions, like those found in the middle of New Mexico in the middle of the winter, you will never see your breath. This is because the air outside has low humidity, and it mixes with your breath so quickly that the resulting mixture is far below saturation, and nothing condenses out.

So how is it that we see our breath on cold days? Because cold air has a low saturation point, and the air in your lungs is 100% saturated. When that warm breath mixes with the cold air, it can hold less water vapor than you’ve just exhaled, so it condenses.

prompt: Is it true you're supposed to put a wet phone in rice? Asking for myself, it's in the rice right now
response:
When my phone fell in the ocean, I panicked and did what everybody says you’re supposed to do: I put it in rice.

I read many, many articles about how this is completely wrong. The rice grains are too big to get in the tiny parts of the phone that need drying. And rice doesn’t absorb moisture well anyway.
