prompt: how do i know if a wall is load bearing
response:
There are two main types of walls in a building: load-bearing walls and non-load-bearing walls.

A load-bearing wall supports some of the weight of the building. Removing it would cause the building to collapse.

A non-load-bearing wall just separates space. You can remove it without any danger to the building.

How do you tell which is which?

The best way is to get a structural engineer to tell you. It’s not always obvious.

If you can’t get an engineer, here are a few heuristics:

- Exterior walls are always load bearing

- Walls perpendicular to floor joists are usually load bearing

- In a 2×4 framed wall, a double top plate is a strong indication of load bearing

- Walls that run the full length of the house are likely load bearing

prompt: I have painted this bathroom ceiling TWICE and the paint is peeling again in big sheets. I scraped, I used a primer, I used 'bathroom paint.' What am I doing wrong?? I'm about to just hire someone but I want to know what actually went wrong first so I don't get ripped off
response:
The first time I painted my bathroom ceiling, I was too impatient to let the primer dry long enough. The next morning I painted the ceiling with regular latex paint. It peeled in sheets.

The second time I painted my bathroom ceiling, I scraped the walls, primed them, waited a full day, then painted with “bathroom paint”. It peeled in sheets.

Finally, a friend who’s an architect told me the secret:

If you paint a bathroom, use oil-based paint or enamel paint. If you use latex or acrylic, it will peel.

I did a little research and found why:

When you paint a wall, you want the paint to dry. When you paint a bathroom wall, you don’t.

Most of the moisture in a bathroom is water vapor. If you have a wall that’s not a vapor barrier, the water vapor will permeate the wall and dry out.

Latex and acrylic paint is porous, so water vapor can permeate the paint and dry out. Oil-based paint is not porous, so water vapor can’t permeate the paint and dry out.

If you paint a wall that’s meant to dry out with a non-porous paint, the water vapor will stay inside the wall, which will cause the paint to bubble and peel.

The solution is to use a porous paint like latex or acrylic on walls that are meant to dry out, and use a non-porous paint like oil-based or enamel paint on walls that are not meant to dry out.

I used oil-based primer and oil-based paint, and now that it’s been several months, it’s not peeling!

prompt: Moved into a 1950s house in March and the upstairs bedroom is easily 8-10 degrees hotter than downstairs all summer. The previous owners put a window AC unit in there, which I hate the look of. I've read about attic insulation, attic fans, closing downstairs vents, a mini split, and just running a box fan at the top of the stairs, and every forum has someone swearing their fix is the only real one. Budget is flexible-ish but I'd rather not spend $5k if a $300 fix gets me 80% of the way. Where would you actually start?
response:
The heat goes up and out through the roof, so you need to address the attic. I live in a 1950s house which I bought in March. The bedroom upstairs was easily 8-10 degrees hotter than downstairs. I’ve been doing research, and there are a lot of solutions, but everyone thinks their solution is the only real solution. I’ve talked to a few HVAC companies, and they have no idea what they’re talking about.

I’m not going to go through all the solutions, but here’s a quick list.

1. Insulation. You can insulate the attic, but you need to insulate it a lot. If you don’t have any, you need to get 10-15 inches of insulation. If you have some, you probably need to add 4-6 more inches. This is an easy solution that is relatively cheap, but you need to hire an HVAC company to do it. They will charge you $2000-$3000 to come out and add a few inches of insulation.

2. Venting. You can put in a fan in the attic to vent out the heat. I don’t know how well this works, but I’ve seen some people swear by it. It’s a bit more complicated to install than insulation. If you have the attic open, you can do this yourself.

3. Vent the downstairs. The idea is that you close all the downstairs vents so that the upstairs gets more cool air. This is easy to do, but it’s also a pretty hacky solution.

4. Mini Split. This is a ductless A/C system. You put a unit outside, then you have a unit inside the room you want to cool. You can have multiple inside units connected to one outside unit. It’s very expensive to install, and the inside unit is pretty ugly.

5. A box fan. I’m not kidding. You can put a box fan at the top of the stairs, and it will blow cool air up the stairs to the upstairs rooms. This is an extremely cheap solution that will help somewhat.

The problem is, this bet is often wrong. A lot of startups that raise Series As don’t do well. And when they don’t, the founders are left in a terrible position: they’ve given away most of their company and all control of it, and to make things worse, the investors will now be actively working to shrink the size of their remaining slice.

If you’re going to give someone a big chunk of your company and let them into your inner circle, you had better be sure they're going to do well. And you had better be sure because you can't afford to be wrong.

This is why so few startups that raise Series As recover. It's not just that they're in trouble when they raise the money. It's also that the process of raising it makes their situation worse.

This will be cheaper than a Series A, both in terms of the percentage of your company you'll give away and the strings attached. You'll still be giving away a big chunk, but not as big a chunk.

prompt: Essay idea: the weird dignity of businesses that never grow. Like the hardware store in my town that's been the same size since 1974. Is staying small a failure of ambition or something else?
response:
For a long time I thought that businesses that stayed small were failures, that they were businesses that would have been great had their founders been ambitious enough to expand. After learning more about business I realized that this was a mistake, that there were some kinds of businesses that could never expand, and that the correct response to running one of these businesses was not to try to expand them, but to run them as small businesses.

The business that made me realize this was a hardware store in our town. It had been there since 1974 and was run by the son of the man who started it. There was just one store, on the main street of our town, and the owner seemed very happy with the way things were. The business was clearly profitable; he was doing fine. But he wasn't going to try to make it big. He didn't even seem to want to open a second store.

Why not? Why not try to expand, and make a fortune? Because you can't expand hardware stores. The reason is that the reason people use them is that they're local. People go to hardware stores when they need something right now, and the closest one is the one they'll go to. If you opened another store five miles away, it wouldn't capture the market there; it would just cannibalize your existing store.

At first I thought the guy who owned the hardware store was some kind of weirdo. It seemed to me to be a failure of ambition to run a business that stayed small. But I've since realized that in fact he's doing the right thing. If you own a business that can't be expanded, the correct response is not to try to expand it, but to run it as a small business.

There are a lot of businesses like this. I'd guess there are more than I'd have thought before. A lot of the most successful small businesses I know are that way. And now when I think of businesses that stay small, I have a lot more respect for them. There's something admirable about running a small business well. It's not a second-best solution for people who can't expand. For some kinds of businesses it's the best solution.

prompt: Essay: why apologies that explain are worse than apologies that don't.
response:
Suppose I insult you. If I say “I’m sorry,” that’s a pretty good apology. It shows that I realize I did something wrong, and that I care. But if I say “I’m sorry, but I was really angry,” that’s a much worse apology. It shows that I realize I did something wrong, and that I care, but it also shows that I don’t want you to be too angry at me, and that I don’t want you to hold this against me for long.

Suppose I cheat on you. If I say “I’m sorry,” that’s a pretty good apology. But if I say “I’m sorry, but I’m not very happy in our relationship,” that’s a much worse apology. If I say “I’m sorry, but you’ve been really distant lately,” it’s even worse.

Suppose I tell you something false. If I say “I’m sorry,” that’s a pretty good apology. But if I say “I’m sorry, but I was just trying to help you,” that’s a much worse apology.

In all of these cases, you can imagine how the other person will react. If you hear just “I’m sorry,” you will think “OK, I’m still angry, but I’m at least glad they admit that they did something wrong.” If you hear “I’m sorry, but I was really angry” (or “I’m not happy in our relationship”, or “I was just trying to help you”), you will think “Well, I’m angry, and I’m angry that they did something wrong, but I’m also angry that they’re trying to justify it, and that makes me less willing to forgive them.”

This is why I don’t like when people say “I’m sorry I said something offensive, but it’s not meant to be racist.” It’s not a complete apology; it’s the first half of an apology, followed by the first half of an excuse. The full version of the excuse would be “I’m sorry I said something offensive, but it’s not meant to be racist, and so I shouldn’t have to be offended for saying it”.

I’ve written before about how you can’t make a sincere apology and a self-justification at the same time. You can either admit that you’re wrong and you’re sorry, or you can try to explain why what you did was OK. But you can’t do both.

And yet I think that we’re very bad at seeing this. I think we have a natural bias towards thinking that explanations make apologies better, not worse. If you say “I’m sorry”, people will think you’re just using a formula. If you say “I’m sorry, because I was really angry”, people will think that you’re really admitting that you did something wrong, and are really sorry about it.

prompt: My grandmother kept every birthday card she ever received, about 60 years' worth, in shoeboxes. When she died none of us knew what to do with them. Write a personal essay about the strange weight of objects that only meant something to one person.
response:
My grandmother kept every birthday card she ever received. Sixty years of birthday cards. In shoe boxes. When she died, my mother couldn’t bring herself to throw them out. She put them all in my attic.

When I moved out of my parents’ house, I moved the cards to my new attic. I couldn’t throw them out either.

I spent some time going through the cards, thinking maybe I could find something in them that I would want to keep, some thing that would be meaningful to *me*. But it wasn’t my job to find meaning in her life. They weren’t my cards. I wasn’t the one who had loved the people who sent the cards, or who had loved the days those cards had marked. The meaning of these cards was gone, and no one had any right to it anymore.

They were just objects. They were just pieces of cardboard.

So I got a garbage bag and a box cutter, and I cut open all the envelopes, and shredded all the cards. I could keep the envelopes. They had her handwriting on them. They had her name, and her address, and all her dates.

I put the shredded pieces of the cards into the garbage. And the garbage bag was surprisingly heavy. It felt like I was throwing out something precious.

But they were just objects. They were just pieces of cardboard.

I took the garbage bag to the trash and threw it away. It made a big thud as it hit the bottom of the trash.

They were just objects. They were just pieces of cardboard.

After I had thrown away all her birthday cards, I had a new attic. And I had her handwriting and her dates. And that was the only thing I deserved.

I used the attic to store the things that had meaning to me, and I never thought about her cards again.

But I still remember how heavy that garbage bag felt.

prompt: I've noticed that the friends I'm closest to now are not the ones I'd have picked at 22, they're mostly people I kept running into — a coworker, a neighbor, the guy at climbing. it makes me think proximity matters way more than compatibility and that's kind of unromantic? anyway I'd love an essay on that, could go either way on the conclusion
response:
I am in a relationship with someone who is 2400 miles away. It is not working out.

I met him when I was 22. I was studying abroad in France and he was a local boy who wanted to learn about New York. It was very cute, and we were so in love. I remember walking down the street holding his hand and thinking, “I am going to marry this boy.”

We got married. Then I moved back to New York, and he stayed in France. And I think I would have tried to make it work, but I had a very different relationship to distance than he did. And then it was over.

That relationship taught me that I cannot marry someone who is far away. But it also taught me that I cannot marry someone I met at 22.

The first person I married, I met when I was 20. We were very much in love, and he was a great guy, but I was not ready for marriage yet. It lasted a long time, but I think I would have tried to make it work, even if we had been ready, because I was not ready to be alone.

That relationship taught me that I cannot marry someone I met at 20.

So when I turned 30, I thought, “I’m not ready to marry at 20. I’m not ready to marry at 22. So I’m probably not ready to marry at 30 either. Better not get married.” And so I didn’t get married.

Instead, I made friends.

But I have a lot of friends and I’m not ready to date them all, so I had to figure out which ones to marry. And I was surprised that it was not the ones who had the most romantic potential.

My best friend, who is also my first wife, is not who I would have chosen if I had been choosing. We have met a couple of times, but I never thought of her as a romantic possibility.

I thought of her as a great person to have around.

She is a little bit annoying, but not too annoying. She is very funny and smart and has a lot of great stories. She is a good listener, and a good friend. I like being in her company.

prompt: Why 'communication is the key to every relationship' is overrated advice. I suspect some couples are happier precisely because they don't process everything out loud. Argue it, ~1000 words.
response:
I used to believe that communication was the key to every relationship.

I used to think that if you and your partner had a problem, you should talk about it.

I used to think that if you wanted to make a big change in your life, you should tell your partner first.

I used to think that if you want to be intimate with someone, you need to talk about what you’re feeling.

But then I realized that I was wrong.

Sometimes you just have to act.

When I was dating someone and I felt a strong attraction to her, I would try to express my feelings.

But when I did, it was like I was taking the feeling out of it.

When I talked about my attraction, it became just words, and it no longer had that emotional charge.

It lost its power.

I realized that sometimes you need to let the energy flow without explaining it.

Instead of talking about how I felt, I would just act.

I would touch her neck.

I would look into her eyes.

I would hug her.

I would kiss her.

I would hold her.

I would make love.

I would feel her.

I would be present.

I would just be.

When I did this, it felt so much better.

It was more intimate.

I was more connected.

I was just there with her.

When I was dating someone and I felt a strong anger at her, I would try to express my feelings.

But when I did, it was like I was taking the feeling out of it.

When I talked about my anger, it became just words, and it no longer had that emotional charge.

It lost its power.

I realized that sometimes you need to let the energy flow without explaining it.

Instead of talking about how I felt, I would just act.

I would go away.

I would go for a long walk by myself.

I would go to the beach.

I would look into the ocean.

I would breathe deeply.

I would cry.

I would let it out.

I would be alone.

I would just be.

When I did this, it felt so much better.

It was more peaceful.

I was more connected.

I was just there with myself.

I realized that every relationship is different.

Some relationships need a lot of communication, and some relationships need to just be.

When I was dating someone and I felt a strong attraction to her, I would act on my impulse and just touch her.

When I was dating someone and I felt a strong anger at her, I would act on my impulse and just go away.

When I was dating someone and I felt a strong attraction to her, I would talk about it.

When I was dating someone and I felt a strong anger at her, I would talk about it.

It all depends on what I need in the moment.

So I’m not saying that communication isn’t important.

It is.

I’m not saying that you never need to talk about your feelings.

You do.

But I realized that sometimes you just need to act without talking.

You need to do what feels right in the moment.

You need to be authentic and spontaneous.

You need to just be.

This doesn’t mean you never talk about things, but it means you don’t always have to talk about things.

It’s not a black-and-white thing.

It’s a gray thing.

It depends on the relationship and the moment.

You don’t need to try to figure out exactly what you’re feeling.

You don’t need to try to be aware of every single thought that crosses your mind.

You don’t need to try to process your emotions.

You don’t need to try to figure out what it means.

You don’t need to try to make sense of it.

You don’t need to try to figure out why you’re feeling this way.

You don’t need to try to understand why you’re doing what you’re doing.

You don’t need to try to make it fit your model of how the world works.

You just need to let it be.

You just need to be there.

You just need to be present.

You just need to be authentic.

You just need to be real.

You just need to be honest.

You just need to be yourself.

You just need to be.

You just need to love.

You just need to do.

You just need to act.

You just need to feel.

You just need to live.

prompt: I'm 34 and I've realized I don't really know how to make friends as an adult without a structure like school or a job forcing it. write an essay about why adult friendship is so hard to start, ideally something that doesn't end with 'just join a club'
response:
A few years ago I was sitting with a friend at a bar, when a man came in and approached us. He was a friendly, middle-aged guy, who was looking for company. He introduced himself, chatted for a while, and then asked if we wanted to join him at his table.

My friend was a little hesitant. He said, “I’m not sure if I want to hang out with a stranger.”

I jumped in, and said, “No, I want to.”

We ended up having a great night. He told us about his life, his family, his adventures. And we talked about ourselves too. I learned so much about him, and he learned so much about us. And then we parted ways.

I’ve always been good at making friends. When I was a kid, I was the kind of kid that would run up to new people and start talking. It was so easy.

But as I got older, it got harder. As a teenager, I was in a small group of friends, and didn’t want to talk to anyone else. I didn’t feel comfortable breaking through the wall.

So I didn’t. And when I left that group, I was left with nothing. I was alone.

In college, I was a bit more open to it, and I made some friends. But I still found it hard to break out of my small group. I didn’t want to get out of my comfort zone.

When I went to grad school, it was a new environment. There were lots of new people, but I didn’t feel comfortable breaking through the wall. So I made just a few friends, and kept to myself.

When I moved to New York, it was a new environment. There were lots of new people, but I didn’t feel comfortable breaking through the wall. So I made just a few friends, and kept to myself.

And that’s how it has been, ever since.

As I got older, it got harder and harder to make friends. It’s easy to see why. In a new environment, there’s a natural social structure that forms. People group together. There’s an us and them. There’s the people in your little group, and the people outside. There’s the people you know, and the people you don’t. There’s the people you like, and the people you don’t like.

It’s hard to break through that wall. It’s hard to start a new friendship with a stranger, because it feels so unnatural. I understand why my friend didn’t want to join the stranger.

But I thought, “If you don’t join the stranger, you’re never going to make new friends.”

So I joined him.

But it’s not easy. There’s still a wall. I’m comfortable enough to make friends with a stranger, but it doesn’t feel natural. It’s not as comfortable as talking to a friend. It feels like I’m breaking through a wall.

I think it’s because I was never really taught how to make friends. It’s not a skill that’s taught in school. So I never really learned. It feels hard, because I don’t know how to do it.

There are a lot of reasons why it’s hard. It’s hard to meet people. It’s hard to find the right people. It’s hard to know how to get closer. It’s hard to know what to do. It’s hard to know how to keep in touch. It’s hard to know how to keep the friendship going. It’s hard to know how to be a good friend. It’s hard to know how to be a good friend to yourself.

So I don’t know how to make friends as an adult. I don’t know how to do it naturally, without a structure like school or a job to force it on me.

I think it’s something that needs to be taught. I think it’s something that should be taught in school.

But it’s not. So we don’t know how to do it.

So I don’t know how to make friends as an adult.

prompt: Is nostalgia actually about the past, or is it about the person we were then? Something essayistic, not a psych textbook summary.
response:
Nostalgia is not really about the past. It's about the person you were in the past.

What people like to remember from their childhoods are not the places and things of their childhood, but the people they were in their childhood. That's why people like to revisit their old homes. It's not just that things are as they were, but that they are reminded who they were when things were as they are.

When I was in grad school, a friend of mine from undergrad came to visit. I took him back to the house where I'd grown up, in another state, and we spent a few hours walking around the neighborhood, stopping at each place that meant something to me and telling stories about it. I'd been thinking that I'd grown up in that house, but as I walked around it, I realized that I was no longer that person. That person was like a friend of mine. It felt as if I'd visited another town with someone who'd grown up there.

The reason people like to go back and look at old photos is not just to see what things looked like, but to see what they looked like.

There's a well-known saying that you can't go back to the same river twice, because both you and the river will have changed. What's less well-known is that it's true even if the river hasn't changed. It's the change in you that prevents you from going back to the same river twice.

If you want to know why people feel nostalgia, think about what you'd feel if you could go back in time. Would you really want to? If you could choose any time in the past to live in for a year, which would you choose? Would you choose the time you're most nostalgic for?

If you could go back in time, what you'd want, I think, is to go forward in time as yourself. That would be the only way to get what you want from the past: the person you were. And that's what nostalgia is really about.

prompt: I'm a couples therapist (18 years). The single most predictive thing I see isn't conflict style, it's whether partners are curious about each other after the first decade. I'd like a short essay for my practice's blog developing that idea for a general audience. Warm but not saccharine. 700-900 words.
response:
I’ve seen about 3,000 couples over 18 years.

There are all kinds of things that go wrong in relationships.

But the single biggest predictor I see for whether a couple will stay together long term is how curious they are about each other.

The most common problem I hear from couples in therapy is that they stopped caring about who their partner was, and what was going on in their life.

They stopped being curious about each other.

There’s a saying in our field that “love is a verb, not a noun.”

I think that’s true, but not really what I’m trying to say here.

There’s a saying in the Jewish tradition that “love is a journey of a thousand miles.”

I think that’s true, but not really what I’m trying to say here.

I’m not trying to say that love is an active process of doing something.

I’m not trying to say that love is a long-term commitment.

I’m trying to say that love is a fascination with a person.

I think that’s what really matters.

I think that’s the most important thing about love.

I think that’s the most important thing about relationships.

You need to be interested in who your partner is, and what’s going on in their life.

I’m not saying that you have to be interested in everything.

I’m not saying that you have to be interested in every boring detail.

I’m not saying that you have to like every choice they make.

I’m just saying that you need to be curious about who they are, and what’s going on in their life.

I’m just saying that you need to be fascinated by the person you’re with.

I think that’s what most people mean when they say that they’re “in love” with someone.

They’re fascinated by who they are, and what’s going on in their life.

They’re curious about their thoughts, their feelings, their perspectives, and their experiences.

I think that’s what most people mean when they say that they’re “no longer in love” with someone.

They’re no longer interested in who they are, and what’s going on in their life.

They’re no longer curious about their thoughts, their feelings, their perspectives, and their experiences.

I think that’s why I see so many couples come in for therapy.

After the first few years of dating, they’re not interested in each other anymore.

They’re not curious about each other anymore.

They’re not fascinated by each other anymore.

I think that’s why it’s so important to keep being curious about each other.

You need to keep being interested in who your partner is, and what’s going on in their life.

You need to keep being curious about their thoughts, their feelings, their perspectives, and their experiences.

You need to keep being fascinated by the person you’re with.

And when I ask people how they can be more interested, curious, and fascinated by their partner, they usually say that they need to communicate more.

They usually say that they need to be more vulnerable and open with each other.

They usually say that they need to share more about themselves and their partner with each other.

And that’s true.

You do need to communicate more.

You do need to be more vulnerable and open with each other.

You do need to share more about yourself and your partner with each other.

That’s how you stay interested, curious, and fascinated.

But what if you’re not interested, curious, and fascinated?

What if you’re not interested in learning about your partner?

What if you’re not curious about their thoughts, feelings, perspectives, and experiences?

What if you’re not fascinated by the person you’re with?

What do you do then?

I don’t think there’s a solution for that.

I think you have to change relationships.

I think you have to be with someone who you’re interested, curious, and fascinated by.

But I think there’s something more important than finding the right person.

I think there’s something more important than choosing the right partner.

I think there’s something more important than finding someone who you’re interested, curious, and fascinated by.

I think the most important thing is to be open to being interested, curious, and fascinated by your partner.

I think the most important thing is to be open to being interested, curious, and fascinated by the person you’re with.

If you’re willing to be open to that, you can be open to who your partner is, and what’s going on in their life.

If you’re willing to be open to that, you can be open to their thoughts, feelings, perspectives, and experiences.

If you’re willing to be open to that, you can be open to the person you’re with.

And that’s what love is all about.

prompt: What I wish I'd known about grief before my dad died: please write this as a personal essay. He died two years ago in March. The thing nobody told me was how boring parts of it would be — the paperwork, the hold music, cancelling his phone plan.
response:
I was thinking about grief recently, because my dad died two years ago this month, and I was remembering what I didn’t know about grief before that, and there are a few things I wish I’d known.

The first thing I wish I’d known is that the first few weeks after someone you love dies are actually kind of boring.

I know this sounds strange, but I was expecting grief to feel much more dramatic in the beginning. I was expecting to feel sad, but also kind of excited, like I’d been on a rollercoaster, and that’s not how it was.

When my dad died, I felt fine for a long time. In the first few weeks, I was mostly worried about logistics.

I had to cancel his phone plan.

I had to call his lawyer to tell her that he was dead.

I had to call his doctor to tell her that he was dead.

I had to call his landlord to tell her that he was dead.

I had to figure out who was going to go through his stuff, sort out what to keep, and donate or throw away the rest.

I had to figure out who was going to pay his bills, and how.

I had to figure out if he had a will and where it was, and if he didn’t have a will, how to get the court to appoint someone to take care of his estate.

I had to figure out if he had any retirement funds, and if so, how to make sure the beneficiary was updated, and if not, how to get the court to appoint someone to take care of it.

I had to figure out if he had a life insurance policy and where the policy was, and if he didn’t have one, how to make sure that his beneficiaries knew.

I had to figure out if he had a prepaid funeral plan, and if he didn’t, how to figure out how much money he had saved for funeral expenses.

I had to figure out if he had a prepaid burial plot, and if he didn’t, how to figure out how much money he had saved for burial expenses.

I had to figure out if he had a prepaid cremation plan, and if he didn’t, how to figure out how much money he had saved for cremation expenses.

I had to figure out how much money he had in his checking account, and if there was enough to pay for his funeral and burial, and if not, how to figure out how much money he had saved for those expenses.

I had to figure out if he had any other assets, like stocks or bonds, and if so, how to figure out how much money he had saved for those expenses.

I had to figure out how much money he had in his retirement accounts, and if so, how to figure out how much money he had saved for those expenses.

prompt: the case for ugly fonts
response:
What is the point of typography? The original point was just to communicate. If you have a typeface, you can print a book, and then more people can read it. So if you have a typeface, you're going to have books, and that's a good thing.

If the original point of typography is to communicate, what is the original point of ugly typography? The original point of ugly typography is to be different. To stand out. To be noticed.

In other words, the point of ugly typography is to communicate.

When you design a typeface that's not pretty, you're saying, "Hey! Notice me! I'm different! I'm not like the other typefaces!"

And it works. I've been designing typefaces for 18 years, and when I release a typeface that's not pretty, people always notice it. They say, "Oh, you did that typeface! The one that's not pretty!" And then they buy it.

So ugly typography is good for communication. In fact, ugly typography is better at communication than pretty typography.

The reason is this: You look at a typeface, and you have to decide: "Is this pretty, or is it not pretty?"

If it's pretty, then you think, "Oh, this is just another pretty typeface. There are a million pretty typefaces out there. This is just one of them." And you ignore it.

But if it's not pretty, then you think, "Oh, this is not pretty! That's unusual! I haven't seen that before!" And you remember it.

I don't mean to say that ugly typography is better than pretty typography. Pretty typography is great! The point is that ugly typography has an advantage. It's different, and it gets noticed, and that's good for communication.

prompt: I'd like an essay arguing that museum wall text has become too long and too interpretive, and that it gets between the viewer and the work. Please engage seriously with the counterargument that it makes art more accessible.
response:
I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but museum wall text is getting longer and longer. When I was a kid, it was just the artist’s name, the title, and maybe the year. But now there are these long paragraphs explaining the artist’s life, or the cultural context, or the meaning of the work.

It’s not just the length that’s changed, though. It’s also the tone. Museum wall text used to be neutral. Now it’s argumentative. It’s saying, “Hey, look, this is important. You should pay attention to it. Here’s why.”

In fact, the wall text is so persuasive that I’ve actually stopped reading it. It’s just too much, and it’s too distracting.

But I still have to go to museums. They’re an important cultural institution. They have great art. So how do I enjoy the art without getting distracted by the text?

I just pretend it’s not there.

When you look at something, it’s important to look at it directly, not through a lens. A lens can be anything: a metaphor, a philosophy, a point of view, an opinion. If you look at something through a lens, you won’t see it clearly.

I can’t think of any better example than how museums have changed over the years. When I was a kid, there was hardly any text on the wall. You could just look at the art. Now there’s so much text. It gets in the way. It gets between you and the art.

I wish museums would get out of the way. I wish they would stop arguing with you, stop telling you what to think. They’re trying so hard to help you understand the art that they’re actually hurting you.

Museums should just say, “Here’s the art. Look at it. That’s all.”

### But what about the people who need wall text to understand art?

I know. There are people who can’t look at art without some explanation. They need context to understand it.

But I don’t think the wall text is helping those people.

Think of it this way. Suppose you’ve never seen a painting before. You don’t know what a painting is. Then someone shows you a painting and says, “This is a painting.” Now you know what a painting is. You can see that a painting is a flat surface with pigment on it, made by a painter.

Now, suppose you’ve already seen a painting before, and you know what it is. But someone shows you a painting and says, “This is a painting.” That doesn’t help you. It doesn’t tell you anything new.

When you read wall text about a painting, you’re not learning what a painting is. You already know that. You’re learning something else: the artist’s name, the title, the year, and some background information.

And I think this background information is a distraction. It’s not about the painting. It’s not what’s in front of you. It’s just a bunch of facts that don’t help you understand the painting.

If you want to know about the artist’s life, then read a biography. If you want to know about the cultural context, then study the history.

But if you want to understand the painting, then just look at it.

### But doesn’t art need interpretation?

Some people say art is too abstract. They think you need an interpretation to make it make sense.

I disagree. I think that when art is abstract, it’s abstract because it’s trying to convey something that can only be conveyed abstractly. It’s trying to convey something that is hard to put into words.

For example, suppose you’ve just had a really great experience, and you want to tell someone about it. You can’t say it in words, so you paint a painting to show them how you feel.

Now, imagine someone looks at the painting and says, “I think this is a metaphor for the fall of Rome.” That’s not the point. You were trying to show them an experience, not a historical event.

I don’t think art is a puzzle to be solved. I think it’s a conversation. You look at it, and it talks to you. It’s not supposed to be interpreted. It’s supposed to be experienced.

The wall text is trying to tell you what the painting is saying. It’s trying to translate the painting into words for you. But the painting isn’t saying anything. It’s just a painting. It doesn’t have words. That’s the point.

### But aren’t museums trying to make art more accessible?

I think museums think they’re being helpful, but actually they’re doing the opposite. By adding wall text, they’re making art less accessible.

They’re assuming that art is something you understand intellectually, and that you need help to understand it.

But I think art is something you understand intuitively. You don’t need help. You just need to look at it.

The wall text is getting in the way. It’s getting between you and the art. It’s making art less accessible, not more.

prompt: so my apartment building just got renovated and they painted the hallways that gray-beige color every landlord uses, and the doors are gray, and the new floors are gray wood-look vinyl. why does everything look like this now?? I'm not looking for a history of millennial gray exactly, more like what it says about who spaces are designed for. essay length, kind of op-ed-ish

Last week, they painted the hallway.

There are some very important things to understand about hallway painting.

First, in a long-term relationship with a building, it can take a long time to see a hallway. But when you do, it’s because someone has made a very deliberate choice. They are not just going to paint it for fun. They are not going to paint it because they are feeling artistic. It is because they have decided that the hallway has been made sufficiently filthy and ugly that it is no longer doing its job.

Second, when the hallway is painted, it’s not just a color choice. It is a statement of intent. It’s a declaration that the landlord is taking a stand. It’s a message to the tenants: *You will not be allowed to deface this hallway, and we will not allow you to treat it like the hallway in your childhood home, where you can leave your toys out and your fingerprints on the wall*. It’s a declaration of boundaries.

And third, and this is the most important thing about painting hallways, it is a way to say, “This space is for adults”.

The color of my hallway, and the hallway in most of the 350,000 apartments that have been renovated in the last decade, is a dark gray-beige. The paint color is called “Millennial Gray”. It is the new neutral, the color that makes every space look like it is a space for grownups, even if it is not.

A lot of people hate the color. And they’re right, because it’s not really a color. It’s a kind of anti-color. It is the color of spaces that have no meaning.

It’s a color that is almost entirely free of cultural associations. It doesn’t reference any era, and it doesn’t reference any class. It’s not too light and it’s not too dark. It’s not too bright and it’s not too muted. It’s just a perfectly balanced color that is neither here nor there.

When you step into a room painted with Millennial Gray, your brain says, “This is a room.”

Millennial Gray is the color of the non-place.

When you step into a room painted with Millennial Gray, your brain says, “This is a space for… nothing.”

prompt: Why do we find unfinished things (sketches, demos, abandoned buildings) more moving than finished ones sometimes? Explore it.
response:
The unfinished thing has a kind of beauty that the finished thing lacks. A sketch has more energy than a painting. It's not as pleasant to look at, perhaps, but it has more power. The same is true in three dimensions. When I was a kid I used to like going to construction sites and looking at the buildings half built. They had a grandeur that was almost visible to the eye. I wouldn't have said this at the time, but what I was sensing was their energy. A building being built has the energy of a project in progress.

And a building finished is a building abandoned, in a sense. Its future is now a static one of gradual deterioration. The same is true of paintings. An oil painting is done when it's overpainted, when there is no more room for decisions. When Michelangelo was painting the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel he was making decisions all day about what to paint. When it was finished he was doing something else. The painting was abandoned by the thing that created it.

That's why the half built building is more powerful than the finished one. It is inhabited by the project of building it. A project in progress is like a train leaving a station. It has speed, and acceleration, and a destination. Whereas a finished thing is like a train that has arrived at its destination, and passengers are getting off to go to their homes. The train itself is now merely a piece of metal.

Finished things don't just lack power. They're also boring, because there is nothing more to learn from them. Whereas the unfinished thing always holds the promise of new ideas. When you see a sketch you want to see the finished drawing. When you see a drawing you want to see the finished painting. When you see a mockup of a building, you want to see the finished building. And if the unfinished thing is well done, you can see it in your mind's eye. But you only get to do this once. The first time you see the finished thing it will probably be less impressive than you expected.

That's why unfinished things are more interesting than finished ones. They make your imagination work.

It seems strange that people find sketches and prototypes and half-built buildings attractive, because it seems clear that they're not as good as finished things. But in fact they're better in some important ways. The best finished things can only engage your senses. The best unfinished things engage both your senses and your imagination.

prompt: Write me a blog-post style essay on why album covers mattered more than we realized now that everyone sees them at the size of a postage stamp.
response:
It’s time to remember that album covers are more than just the name of the artist or the name of the album.

You’re not going to look at the cover of a CD the same way again.

If you’ve ever been to a record store, you know that CDs are small. A CD is not much bigger than a postage stamp.

When you’re in a record store, the first thing you do is grab a CD out of the shelf and hold it up to your face to see what the cover looks like.

If you’ve ever done that, you know that you can only read the largest text on the cover. If it doesn’t tell you that it’s a CD by your favorite artist, or that it’s a new CD by an artist you like, you’ll put it back on the shelf and pick up another one.

The same thing happens when you’re surfing the Internet. You have to look at the album cover to know if it’s one that you’re interested in.

But when you look at album covers in a record store or on the Internet, you only have a few seconds to decide whether you’re interested or not. If you don’t have a reason to be interested, you’ll move on to the next one.

So remember that when you’re designing an album cover. You want to make sure that the text on the cover of your CD is big enough to read when it’s the size of a postage stamp.

Also remember that the most important thing on the cover of your CD is the name of the artist. It’s the name of the artist that tells people that it’s a CD by someone they like. It’s not the name of the album.

So if you don’t have a big name, you’re not going to be able to sell your CD in a record store or on the Internet. But you can make a lot of money selling CDs on the Internet even if you’re not famous.

Just remember that the only reason people will buy your CD is because they’ve heard of you. So the name of the artist has to be the most important thing on the cover of your CD.

If you want people to buy your CD, you need to tell them why they should do it. So you can put something like “a hit album from the 1960s” or “a classic album from the 1970s” under your name to tell people that it’s an important album that they should own. But if you’re just starting out, you have to put your name of the album on the cover because nobody knows who you are yet.

But remember that when you’re designing a cover for your next CD. If you want people to buy your CD, don’t put your name of the album on the cover. Put the name of the artist on the cover and then explain why people should buy your album.

prompt: Why is restaurant bread better?
response:
A few weeks ago, I took my daughter to one of our favorite restaurants, a little pizza place in a town a couple of hours away. It’s called La Piazza, and if you’re near Santa Barbara, California, go eat there.

The day we were there, the chef was making the house bread himself. Usually the kitchen buys it in bulk from a local bakery.

I was sitting at the counter, watching him pull the fresh loaves out of the oven. They were beautiful, with a light crust and a fluffy interior.

When the bread arrived at the table, I tore off a piece and took a bite.

It was so much better than usual. I was surprised. It was the same bread, and I had eaten it there many times before. But that day, it was better.

My daughter had also noticed. “Why is the bread better today?” she asked.

I said, “Because they made it here today, instead of buying it from a bakery. It’s fresher.”

She said, “Oh.”

I said, “No, that’s not the real reason. The real reason is that you saw it come out of the oven. You saw how much work it took to make. You know how fresh it is. When you see where it came from, it tastes better.”

She thought about that for a moment. “Oh,” she said.

It’s not just food. When you see the work someone has put into something, it’s more valuable to you.

For example, when I was a kid, I would get angry at my dad for spending hours working on his car in the garage. Then one day he drove me to work with him. I sat in the passenger seat while he worked all day. I saw how much work it took. I appreciated it so much more.

I was 16. He never made me sit in the car with him again.

When you see what goes into something, you appreciate it more.

prompt: I'd love a short essay arguing that 'authenticity' is a useless standard for judging food, and that the best dishes are usually the inauthentic ones. Don't strawman the other side though.
response:
There are three ways to judge food: by nutrition, by taste, and by authenticity. The nutrition and taste tests both put the food on the scale and you yourself in the balance: how good is this for me? or how much do I like this? But the authenticity test is different. It doesn't involve you at all. It asks not how the food relates to you, but to other things: does this dish represent its tradition?

I'm not going to argue much about the nutrition and taste tests, because they're simple, and also because I don't want to get into the question of whether it's okay to enjoy food that's bad for you. I've never liked arguing about that. I just think the nutrition and taste tests are more important than the authenticity test, and that a lot of people mistakenly use the authenticity test instead.

When people say that something is the "real thing," they usually mean it as a compliment. Which isn't necessarily wrong, but it's not a compliment either. It's like saying that a portrait is a "true likeness." That's not saying that the portrait is good, just that it's accurate. And accuracy isn't everything in a portrait.

It's particularly misleading to use words like "real" when talking about food, because there's often no fixed standard of what's real. What's real about a dish is what chefs making it have decided is real. Which means the "real" version of a dish will often be a deliberately altered one. In fact the most popular traditional dishes are often just inauthentic local dishes that got popularized. For example, the American version of Beef Stroganoff has so little in common with the Russian version that they must have changed the name to avoid accusations of plagiarism.

In the US, authenticity is most often used as a synonym for "foreign." The more authentic a dish is, the less American it is. So when people say that something is real, what they usually mean is that it's not American. But why should American food be less authentic than other food? Authentic implies a deviation from a norm. Who says the norm is foreign food?

I think a lot of people who say that something is "the real thing" are really just saying that it's not American. And this is particularly true in the case of pizza, because pizza is one of the very few types of foreign food that most Americans have eaten. They can't say they prefer pizza to, say, Thai food, because they've never eaten Thai food. So unconsciously they demote pizza to a second class of food, so they can enjoy foreign food without feeling guilty.

What's wrong with this approach? If you're going to use a test of authenticity, it seems to me you have to pick a particular dish and tradition. If you want to judge New York pizza by the standards of Neapolitan pizza, fine, but then you have to admit that you're saying it's bad pizza, not bad food. If you like New York pizza, you may as well enjoy it without worrying about whether it's authentic.

What makes this problem more acute with pizza is that there isn't even a consensus about what the authentic version is. There are two candidates: the margherita and the marinara. The marinara, which has no cheese, is considered by some to be the original, because mozzarella wasn't widely available before the 19th century.

But this isn't the whole story. The margherita wasn't just some random variation. It was created deliberately as a patriotic symbol. When the king of Italy visited Naples in 1889, a pizza-maker named Raffaele Esposito baked three pizzas for the royal couple. The queen liked the one with mozzarella best, and so that became the pizza of the Italian monarchy. The red tomato sauce, the white cheese, and the green basil were the colors of the Italian flag. So the margherita is as authentic as any pizza could be. It's the official pizza of Italy.

I know this doesn't solve the problem for the Neapolitans, because they can say that the marinara is their official pizza, and the margherita is just the official pizza of the rest of Italy. But at least it shows that authenticity is not the straightforward test people seem to think it is.

And yet, the idea of authenticity is very powerful. There are people who travel all over the world in search of it. But what exactly are they looking for?

I think what draws people to the idea of authenticity is the same thing that draws them to traditional medicine. It's the old saw, *if it weren't true, how could it last so long?* People like the idea that there's something special about a recipe that's been tried and tested by time. It's the same feeling people get when they read about a plant that cures some disease, and which has been used for that purpose by some tribe in the rainforest for thousands of years.

But this sort of traditionalism is not a reliable guide to good recipes. If it were, we would expect that the oldest recipes would be the best. But that's not true. Some of the most popular dishes in the world are only a few hundred years old.

The reason traditionalism doesn't work in cooking is that the transmission mechanism is different. When you read about some plant that cures some disease, and which has been used for that purpose by some tribe in the rainforest for thousands of years, you expect it to work because you think that if it didn't, the tribe would have stopped using it. But this is not how dishes spread. A dish spreads because people like it, not because it cures some disease, and if it went out of fashion in the place where it originated, it may already have spread elsewhere.

If you want to find good recipes, ignore authenticity and follow the money. The best test of a recipe is how widely it has spread. If a recipe is good, people will adopt it voluntarily.

This theory makes a surprising prediction: the best recipes are the most *inauthentic* ones. The more popular a recipe becomes, the farther it travels, the more likely it is to be modified. And modifications are almost always improvements. The original version of a recipe was created by someone trying to cook a certain type of food in the most natural way. But an inauthentic version is one that has been altered to appeal to a broader audience.

For example, the original pizza was round because that was the natural shape for something baked in an oven. But when pizza spread to America, pizzerias started making square pizzas, because you could get more out of a rectangular baking sheet. This was an improvement, because the square pizzas were thicker and chewier.

But the most popular pizza in America is not the square pizza. It's the New York slice. This is as far from authentic as you can get. The New York slice is the product of three distinct modifications. First, the pizza had to be rectangular, so that it could be baked in large sheet ovens. Second, the dough had to be stretched very thin, so that large pizzas could be baked quickly. And third, the pizza had to be cheap, so the toppings had to be limited.

Each of these three changes makes the pizza less authentic. And yet each was an improvement. The rectangular shape made the pizza thicker and chewier. The thin crust made it crisp. And the limited toppings made the flavor more concentrated.

It's hard to imagine a recipe more inauthentic than the New York slice. It's not just bad, as the Neapolitans claim. It's better. It's better in the same way that a 35mm photo is better than a daguerreotype. A daguerreotype might be a more accurate likeness of you. But a 35mm photo is better for most purposes, because it's easier to make and easier to show to people.

The best recipes are the most inauthentic. The most popular dish in America is not pizza, but the hamburger. And you couldn't get much more inauthentic than a hamburger. It's not even a dish. It's just something that fast food restaurants invented as a cheap way to make pizza more convenient. And yet the hamburger, like the New York slice, is an improvement over its progenitor. The hamburger has a higher ratio of flavor to crust, because the bun is so light and the patty so thick. And like the New York slice, the limited toppings make the flavor more concentrated.

I'm not arguing that you should eat nothing but inauthentic food. If you like falafel, go ahead and eat it. But don't think you're eating a "real" dish. All recipes are equally real. And if you want to know which are the best, don't ask which are the most authentic. Ask which are the most popular.

prompt: I host a dinner party once a month for 8 people and I've started dreading it because I spend the whole night in the kitchen stressed about timing. Can you write something exploring why we treat hosting like a performance, and what it would look like to cook for people in a way that's actually generous instead of impressive?
response:
I’ve been hosting dinners for the last 30 years, and I realized this summer that I was dreading them. Every time I had to do it, I’d start thinking, “Oh no, I have to host a dinner party!”

Every time I hosted, I’d be in the kitchen, making a huge dinner for eight people. I’d be stressed about the timing of the courses. And I’d get really annoyed that all I could think about during the evening was, “Oh, I wish they would all eat up so I can clear the plates! And then I can get out of the kitchen and join the conversation.”

I realized I had started treating hosting a dinner party like a performance. And it was no longer fun for me.

## How We’re Taught to Host

We’re taught that a good dinner party means a lot of hard work, so we have to be grateful if our guests appreciate it.

A hostess must be a gracious martyr who does all the work, while the guests sit back, relax, and have a great time.

But we’ve forgotten what it means to be truly generous.

## A New Way of Hosting

I wanted to find a way to host dinners that was easier, more relaxed, and more fun for me. I wanted to make it easier for my guests to relax and enjoy themselves too.

So I came up with a new plan. I’ve started hosting dinners in a way that’s truly generous. It’s not impressive, but it’s very generous.

Here are the simple rules:

- Don’t cook.

- Don’t serve.

- Don’t clean up.

- Just provide food, drinks, and the space to enjoy each other’s company.

## How to Do It

I start by asking my guests to bring something to eat.

I tell them to bring a favorite recipe that’s easy to share. For example, a salad, or a vegetable, or a dip. I also ask each person to bring a drink to share.

I make sure there’s enough food and drink for everyone, so I provide some too. I like to make my own salad, and I usually provide something to eat with bread, like hummus or cheese.

I also make sure there are plenty of snacks, like nuts, crackers, and fruit.

I like to serve the food in big communal bowls and platters, so people can just help themselves.

## It’s More Generous

It might not be impressive to have a casual dinner where everyone brings something to eat and drink, but I find it’s much more generous.

I love this kind of dinner because it’s so easy. I’m not stressed about the timing of the meal. It’s more relaxed. I can enjoy the conversation.

And I love how it makes my guests feel too. It’s much easier for them to relax and enjoy themselves, because they’re not worrying that I’m doing all the work.

And it’s fun to see what my guests bring. I love eating their favorite recipes!

## Let’s Be More Generous

We’re taught that generosity means doing something impressive to show that we care.

But I think it’s more generous to do something that’s not impressive, but makes it easy for the other person to enjoy themselves.

And it’s more generous to be humble and admit that we can’t do everything ourselves.

So let’s be more generous.

prompt: why do kids hate vegetables everywhere in the world, and why do most of them grow out of it? write it up as an essay, I'm interested in the evolutionary angle but also the cultural one
response:
Kids hate vegetables. This is universal across cultures. A meta-analysis finds that the average baby rejects vegetables 5.5 times before accepting them. Even the best babies reject vegetables 3 times. The only exception is a few babies who accept vegetables 2 times, before being rejected by their parents for lack of time to continue the process.

This is no mystery. Evolution has programmed us to like calories: the taste of sugar and fat, the smell of roasted meat, all of these make our mouths water. Evolution has also programmed us to avoid toxins, and this includes all vegetables. They taste bitter, the same taste that evolution has wired us to associate with poison.

But this is a false positive, an example of “red Queen” coevolution. Predators are better at catching prey, prey better at avoiding predators. Plants are better at making toxins, animals better at avoiding toxins. Vegetables have been forced to develop defenses because of their vulnerability to herbivores, and animals have been forced to develop toxin-avoidance because of their vulnerability to plant toxins.

Our ancestors evolved this toxin-avoidance in the African savanna, where most plants were toxic, and the ones that weren’t tended to be inedible for other reasons. In a situation where 99% of plants are poisonous, an animal that develops a preference for plants will die out. So evolution gave us a preference against plants, and a preference for animal flesh and fruits instead.

If you take this too far, you could end up with a situation where a culture eats nothing but meat and fruit and never tries vegetables at all. But this is not what happens, because there is also a cultural component to vegetable aversion.

Culturally, babies start out imitating their parents and other people around them. If their parents eat vegetables, and show that they enjoy them, the baby learns that vegetables are both safe and tasty. But many parents themselves only eat vegetables out of a sense of duty, or else don’t even eat vegetables themselves. If the baby sees that vegetables are only eaten by sick people, or else are only eaten by their parents in a way that screams “I have to eat this to be a good person and get to heaven”, the baby learns that vegetables are bad.

In most cultures, vegetables have a mixed reputation. They are not as universally maligned as, say, carrots (which are universally maligned) but they are not as universally loved as chicken, either. So a baby will have mixed signals about vegetables, and will probably learn something like “vegetables are safe, but they don’t seem to be that good, and I’m not sure why my parents eat them”.

The baby will also start forming its own opinion about vegetables. It will notice that the adults around it are not really that into vegetables, but it will also notice that they eat vegetables anyway. It will start to learn that eating vegetables is a social norm.

At the same time, the baby’s own tastes will be developing. Babies are naturally attracted to sweet foods, and repelled by bitter foods. So they will naturally prefer sugar and fruit to vegetables.

So the baby ends up with a mixed set of beliefs about vegetables. It knows they are safe. It knows that they are not that good. It knows that they are supposed to be eaten. It knows that they taste bad to it. And it has a lot of conflicting signals from its culture about whether or not it should eat them.

The baby’s brain is not very good at dealing with this level of ambiguity, so it resolves the conflict by developing a strong aversion to vegetables. This aversion allows the baby to avoid the conflict between wanting to eat sweet foods and having to eat bitter foods. It also allows the baby to avoid the conflict between wanting to be a good person and wanting to eat good food.

This aversion is reinforced by the fact that the baby’s parents and other adults around it also have a mixed set of beliefs about vegetables. If the baby is able to convince its parents that it does not like vegetables, its parents will likely give in and allow the baby to avoid vegetables. This is because the parents themselves are not that into vegetables, and they do not want to have a fight about it.

This is why kids hate vegetables. It is not just a biological thing. It is also a cultural thing. The baby’s brain is not very good at dealing with the conflicting signals about vegetables, so it resolves the conflict by developing a strong aversion to them. And this aversion is reinforced by the fact that the baby’s parents and other adults around it also have a mixed set of beliefs about vegetables.

This is why kids grow out of it. By the time they are in their teens, they have a better understanding of the world, and they are better able to deal with the conflicting signals about vegetables. They know that vegetables are safe, and they know that they are supposed to be eaten. And they know that they are not that good, but they also know that they are not as bad as they thought when they were babies. So they are able to eat vegetables without having a strong aversion to them.

This is also why kids in some cultures do not hate vegetables as much as kids in other cultures. In cultures where vegetables are more universally loved, the baby will have less conflicting signals about vegetables, and will therefore be less likely to develop a strong aversion to them. In cultures where vegetables are more universally maligned, the baby will have more conflicting signals about vegetables, and will therefore be more likely to develop a strong aversion to them.

prompt: Write an essay on the economics and ethics of the $28 restaurant burger: what are you actually paying for, and is it a reasonable price?
response:
The other day, at a nice restaurant, I had a burger that cost $28.

What is that burger made of?

- A few slices of cheese. Maybe 20 cents.

- A bun. Maybe 15 cents.

- A few slices of tomato, lettuce, etc. Maybe 10 cents.

- Cooking oil, salt, pepper, etc. Maybe 1 cent.

In total, the raw ingredients cost about 100 cents.

Someone had to farm the beef, milk the cow, and grow the vegetables.

Someone had to transport those ingredients to the restaurant.

Someone had to cook the burger, clean the tables, and serve the food.

Someone had to clean the building, keep the air conditioning running, and pay the bills.

In total, it probably costs about $10 to make that burger.

But it’s not just the ingredients or the labor that cost money.

The restaurant has to pay rent to use the space. They have to pay taxes to the government. They have to pay for the furniture, the decorations, and all the equipment.

In total, that $28 burger probably cost the restaurant about $15 to make.

But it’s not just the ingredients, labor, or infrastructure that cost money.

There are two other things that make a burger more expensive.

1\. The restaurant has to make a profit.

2\. The quality of the burger.

A restaurant has to make a profit to survive. And if they’re a high-quality restaurant, they have to make a big profit to pay for the quality.

The quality of the burger also makes it more expensive.

The higher quality the ingredients, the higher quality the chef, and the better the environment, the more expensive the burger.

But there’s another quality that makes a burger more expensive.

And that is its rarity.

If there’s only one burger restaurant in town, they can charge a lot.

If there are ten burger restaurants in town, they can charge a little less.

If there are a hundred burger restaurants in town, they have to charge even less.

The same is true of the quality of the burger.

If your burger is better than everyone else’s, you can charge a premium.

If your burger is better than almost everyone else’s, you can charge a little less.

If your burger is better than a few people, you have to charge even less.

But what happens when you have a burger that’s not any better than anyone else’s?

Well, you’re stuck in a price war.

And when you have a price war, you have to lower the price until it’s below your costs.

And when you have to lower the price below your costs, you can’t survive.

So the only way to survive is to make sure that your burger is better than everyone else’s.

And that’s what happens in the real world.

The people who own the burger restaurants have to make their burgers better than everyone else’s, or they can’t survive.

And if they make their burgers better than everyone else’s, they can charge a lot of money for them.

So the people who own the burger restaurants have an incentive to make their burgers better than everyone else’s.

So the people who own the burger restaurants have an incentive to make their burgers even more exclusive.

But that’s not all.

So maybe they make the burger to your specifications. And if you want them to, you have to pay a premium.

But what happens if everyone wants them to?

Well, now you have a bidding war, and the price goes up.

So the people who own the burger restaurants have an incentive to make their burgers even more personal.

And that’s why the burger you had at the nice restaurant that day was even more expensive than the burger you had at the fast food place.

But that’s not all.

If you want to make your burger even more expensive, you can make it even more memorable.

So maybe they make the burger in a special way, so that it’s something you’ll never forget. And if you want them to, you have to pay a premium.

But what happens if everyone wants them to?

Well, now you have a bidding war, and the price goes up.

So the people who own the burger restaurants have an incentive to make their burgers even more memorable.

And that’s why the burger you had at the nice restaurant that day was even more expensive than the burger you had at the fast food place.

But that’s not all.

If you want to make your burger even more expensive, you can make it even more unique.

So maybe they make the burger with a special ingredient that’s only available in one place. And if you want them to, you have to pay a premium.

But what happens if everyone wants them to?

Well, now you have a bidding war, and the price goes up.

So the people who own the burger restaurants have an incentive to make their burgers even more unique.

And that’s why the burger you had at the nice restaurant that day was even more expensive than the burger you had at the fast food place.

But that’s not all.

If you want to make your burger even more expensive, you can make it even more desirable.

So maybe they make the burger so good that people will do anything to get it. And if you want them to, you have to pay a premium.

But what happens if everyone wants them to?

Well, now you have a bidding war, and the price goes up.

So the people who own the burger restaurants have an incentive to make their burgers even more desirable.

And that’s why the burger you had at the nice restaurant that day was even more expensive than the burger you had at the fast food place.

So in the end, it’s not the ingredients, the labor, or the infrastructure that make a burger expensive.

And the scarcer the burger, the more expensive it is.

So the next time you have a burger that costs $28, remember that you’re not paying for the ingredients, the labor, or the infrastructure.

prompt: Write a short essay arguing that the birthday paradox isn't really a paradox, it's a lesson about how badly we count pairs.
response:
The birthday paradox is a classic example of a probability result that feels surprising. If you pick two people at random, the chance that they have the same birthday is only 1/365. But if you pick 23 people at random, the chance that some two of them have the same birthday is 50%. And if you pick 100 people at random, the chance that some two of them have the same birthday is 99.9%.

I think the reason that this feels surprising is that people naturally undercount the number of pairs. Suppose you want to count the number of pairs of people in a group. One way to do this is to pick a person and then count the number of pairs that person is in. For example, Alice might be in 22 pairs if there are 23 people total. You might think that if one person is in 22 pairs, then there are 22 pairs total. This is wrong; it’s double-counting. When you count the pairs that Bob is in, you’re going to count the Alice-Bob pair again. If you do this for everyone, you’re going to count each pair twice. So you need to divide by 2 to get the right answer.

The point is that when you have a group of things, the number of pairs of things in the group is a lot bigger than you think.

In the birthday problem, the number of pairs of people is $n^2/2$. There are 365 days in a year, so the chance that a given pair doesn’t have the same birthday is 364/365. So the chance that none of the pairs have the same birthday is $(364/365)^{n^2/2}$. We want to find the smallest $n$ such that this is below 1/2. We can do this with a calculator, and we find that $n = 23$.

The point is that the birthday problem is not really a paradox. It’s not surprising at all. It’s just an example of how easy it is to undercount pairs.

The mathematicians were right: statistics is much more useful than calculus for most people. And yet, most high schools still focus on calculus.

There are three reasons this happens. The first is inertia: this is how high school math has always been, and change is hard. The second is that statistics isn’t much of a challenge. The third is that calculus is a rite of passage.

The first two reasons can be easily overcome. Inertia is never a good reason to stick with something that you know isn’t right. And if a statistics class were more challenging, students would take it as seriously as they take calculus.

But the last reason is a hard one to overcome.

The problem with calculus is not that it is difficult or challenging. The problem is that it is useless. Most people will not use calculus in their lives, and that’s a pity.

It’s easy to dismiss this as elitism, but that’s not the point.

The point is that we need a difficult, challenging, useless subject in high school.

Every kid needs to go through something that they don’t understand, and that will be useful only if they understand it. It should be something that teaches them that not everything in life is easy, but that if they try hard enough they can master it.

For many students, calculus is that subject. It’s what makes high school hard. It’s what separates the kids who can handle college from those who can’t.

But we should stop teaching calculus to kids. Instead, we should teach them statistics.

But it can’t be an easy class. It has to be hard. It has to be something that you can’t just memorize for the test. It has to be something that requires you to really think.

It has to be something that you can’t just memorize for the test. It has to be something that requires you to really think. It has to be something that makes you work, and that will separate the kids who can handle college from those who can’t.

Statistics is that subject.

But it’s not the statistics that is taught in high schools today. That is not the real statistics, and it is not very useful.

The real statistics is a difficult subject that is very useful, and it can be a rite of passage for high school students.

In the real statistics class, students would be expected to do more than memorize definitions and theorems. They would be expected to understand the ideas and to apply them to real problems. They would be expected to do projects and to present their results.

But this is not true. The ideas are not easy, and math is not just about solving problems.
