prompt: Why does everyone have a junk drawer? Write a playful but genuinely thoughtful essay about it.
response:
A few years ago, I was visiting my grandmother’s house.

My grandmother was 87 years old, and had spent most of her life in the same house.

My mom, dad, and I were sitting in her living room, talking and laughing, when she said, “I think I need to clean out that junk drawer.”

She got up, walked into the kitchen, and opened the junk drawer.

It had pencils, batteries, paper clips, coins, stickers, rubber bands, and other miscellaneous things.

She said, “I’m going to throw away everything in here.”

She took out the contents of the junk drawer, and walked to the trash can.

But then she noticed a pencil was in there.

She stopped, and said, “Wait, we can’t throw away the pencil! That’s useful!”

She went back to the junk drawer and put the pencil in it.

She took out the contents of the junk drawer, and walked to the trash can.

But then she noticed some batteries were in there.

She stopped, and said, “Wait, we can’t throw away the batteries! That’s useful!”

She went back to the junk drawer and put the batteries in it.

She took out the contents of the junk drawer, and walked to the trash can.

But then she noticed a few coins were in there.

She stopped, and said, “Wait, we can’t throw away the coins! That’s useful!”

She went back to the junk drawer and put the coins in it.

After doing this with a few other things, she said, “Okay, I guess that junk drawer isn’t so bad after all. It’s not really junk.”

And then she went back to sitting in the living room, talking and laughing.

I think about this story a lot.

Everyone has a junk drawer.

It’s the place for all the random things that might be useful someday.

It’s the place for all the things that don’t have a place.

But really, it’s the place for all the things that have a place.

You might think of it as a junk drawer, but it’s really a treasure drawer.

Every time you throw something away, you feel a little bit of regret.

Every time you throw something away, you feel a little bit of guilt.

That’s why we have junk drawers.

So we can feel good about keeping things that might be useful someday.

We don’t have junk drawers to throw things away.

We have junk drawers to keep things from throwing them away.

We have junk drawers to feel good about keeping things.

When you have a junk drawer, you feel good about keeping things.

When you don’t have a junk drawer, you feel bad about keeping things.

So we have junk drawers.

It’s the place where we can keep everything that’s still useful.

But it’s not the only place.

Everyone has more than one junk drawer.

Everyone has a junk drawer in their computer.

Everyone has a junk drawer in their phone.

Everyone has a junk drawer in their mind.

Everything you haven’t forgotten is in a junk drawer.

It’s all there, ready to be used someday.

That’s why we have junk drawers.

So we can feel good about keeping things.

So we don’t have to throw anything away.

So we can remember that everything has a place.

So we can remember that everything is still useful.

And so we can remember that everything is still important.

prompt: Write an essay about learning to sharpen kitchen knives as an adult, and what it taught you about patience. I know you don't have hands, just write it as if from a home cook who finally figured it out after ruining two cheap knives.
response:
A few years ago I read the *New York Times* cookbook. It was a book of recipes and tips written by the paper’s food columnist, who was also the author of a book called *At Home: A Cookbook* (which I have not yet read).

One of the tips I found in the cookbook was on how to sharpen knives. I’d been sharpening knives in a way that was, at best, ineffective. So, I tried her method and it actually worked. It was the best thing that could have happened. I had knives that were sharp again!

I learned that there are two parts to sharpening a knife. The first is to make sure that the blade is true and straight. If the blade has a big nick in it or has been bent out of shape, you can’t sharpen it. It has to be straight. This is called honing. The second is to grind a sharp edge into the blade. This is called sharpening.

I sharpened my knives, but I did it wrong. The result was a dull knife with a curved edge. After a year or so I had two knives that were pretty useless, and I decided to throw them away.

I went out and bought two cheap knives that were sharp out of the box. I was going to be careful not to ruin these.

A few years later, I read an essay about sharpening knives on a blog called *Cooking for Engineers*. It was the best explanation I’ve read on the topic, and it made me realize that I’d been sharpening knives wrong all along.

This was not a good feeling, because I had ruined two knives. They are both sharp again now, but it took me a long time to figure it out.

The key thing I had been doing wrong was sharpening the knife all the way to the tip. This is bad because the tip of the knife is thinner than the rest of the blade. If you sharpen the whole blade the same way, you’ll make the tip of the blade thinner. This is bad. The author of *Cooking for Engineers* says that you should only sharpen a knife up to about 1/4 inch from the tip.

I sharpened my knives, and now they’re sharp again. They’ve been sharp for about a year now. I sharpen them every month or so.

This is a small thing. But learning to sharpen knives, for me, was an important lesson in patience.

I’d been doing it wrong for years. I could see that something was wrong with my knives, but I didn’t realize what. I’d gotten so accustomed to having dull knives that I hadn’t spent much time figuring out why they were dull.

Learning to sharpen knives made me more patient. When I’m doing something wrong, I’m more likely to take the time to figure out why it’s wrong.

There’s another lesson I’ve learned from sharpening knives. It’s that sharpening knives is a good way to spend 10 minutes. I do it after I wash the dishes. I sharpen my knives and put them away. It’s a good time to be alone with my thoughts.

prompt: thesis: most home maintenance disasters (rot, mold, foundation cracks) come down to water going somewhere you didn't notice. turn that into a short essay a new homeowner would actually read
response:
A few months ago, my wife and I bought a house. It's very nice. But it is also not perfect.

The first thing we noticed was that the basement was a bit flooded. There was water up to the ankle in a few places.

There was also a bit of a crack in the wall.

My wife, who is not the sort of person to be phased by ankle-deep water, was a little more concerned.

The water was coming from a pipe. The pipe was leaking.

My wife was right. We should be concerned. Pipes leak all the time. If left unchecked, they can cause huge problems. So we called a plumber.

He came over, looked at the pipe, and said that we needed to get it replaced. He recommended a local company to do the work.

The plumber's guy came over, and looked at the pipe, and said that we needed to get it replaced.

He dug a trench, replaced the pipe, and filled the trench back in.

And that was that.

The next day, the grass in the trench was dead. We figured that was normal. After all, we'd dug it up, so, yeah, it's probably going to die.

A few days later, the grass around the trench had died, too. We figured that was normal, too.

A week later, the entire front lawn was dead. We figured that was not normal.

We talked to a few different people. We got a few different theories. We were not sure which one was right. So we decided to dig.

We dug and dug and dug and dug, trying to find where the line was that separated the dead grass from the living grass.

When we dug enough, we found something.

There was a hole in the ground. It was not the hole that the pipe was in. It was a completely different hole.

We poked around and found out what it was. It was the ground-level drainage pipe for the house. It was supposed to carry the water away from the house. Instead, it was clogged up and not doing its job.

The water was going into the ground instead of away from the house. It was flooding the front yard.

We were relieved. We now knew exactly what the problem was, and how to fix it.

We called the plumber again. He dug up the drainage pipe, cleaned it out, and put it back in.

The grass grew back. The basement dried out. The crack in the wall didn't get any worse.

The water was going somewhere we didn't expect, and it was causing problems. Once we knew where the water was going, we were able to fix the problem.

A lot of house problems are water problems.

The house is full of pipes. Pipes carry water. They can get clogged or leak. Water can go somewhere unexpected. Then something can rot or grow or crack.

A lot of the time, if you understand where the water is going, you can fix the problem.

prompt: Write a piece in the style of a reflective blog post on why measuring twice and cutting once is good advice that almost nobody follows, and what that says about how we actually learn practical skills.
response:
My father had a saying: “measure twice, cut once.” He said it every time I was doing some sort of manual labor. It was his way of saying, “Be more careful.”

I learned this lesson in a very practical way. I was working as a carpenter, and I was asked to make a wooden frame, like a picture frame, out of 1×6 boards.

I measured the lengths I needed, cut the boards, and then put them all together. But when I was done, I realized I’d made a mistake. I’d been measuring the *outside* of the frame, but that was wrong. I needed to measure the *inside*.

So I took the frame apart, and measured the boards again, and cut them again, and put them back together. This time I made the frame the right size.

The lesson I learned from this is that there is a lot of value in checking your work. But not just checking your work once. I checked my work once, and found out it was wrong. It’s only by checking your work a *second* time that you can be sure it’s correct.

The point of the saying “measure twice, cut once” is not to measure twice. It’s to *cut once*. It’s about saving time. If you cut the board twice, you throw away one board, which takes a lot more time to cut than it takes to measure. So by measuring twice, you save time.

There’s a lot of value in this principle. It’s easy to check your work. But the value isn’t in checking your work. The value is in *saving time* by not having to redo your work.

### The value of checking your work

For example, I used to write a lot of shell scripts, and I would sometimes make a mistake and accidentally delete all the files in a directory. I would say `rm *`, when I meant to say `rm *.log`.

So I started to make it a habit to always check what I was doing before I ran a command. I would hit the up arrow to go back to my last command, and then change it, so it would display what I was about to do.

Like I would type

```
rm *.log
```

and then hit up arrow, to see what I just typed, and then hit enter.

This is such an easy thing to do! It takes less than a second, and it’s so simple that it can be second nature. But it’s so valuable! If you make it a habit to check your work, you won’t delete all the files in a directory by accident.

### It’s hard to learn practical skills

I think one of the hardest things about learning is learning practical skills. The kind of skills that save you time. For example, I mentioned last week that the best way to learn how to program is by reading a book that teaches you a practical skill, like how to build a web application in Ruby.

If you read a book that teaches you how to program in Ruby, you’ll learn how to program. But if you read a book that teaches you how to program in Python, you’ll learn *more* than just how to program. You’ll also learn how to use the Python standard library, which will save you a lot of time.

I’m not saying you shouldn’t learn theory. I think it’s important to learn theory, but it’s also important to learn practical skills, because it can save you a lot of time.

But I think we don’t pay enough attention to learning practical skills.

### “measure twice, cut once” is a practical skill

I think a big problem is that a lot of people don’t pay attention to these things because they don’t see the value in them.

For example, my father kept saying to me, “measure twice, cut once”, and I thought, “Well, duh. I know that.” But I didn’t understand that there’s actually a lot of value in that.

So I kept making mistakes.

But if you realize that there’s a lot of value in checking your work, and you practice it, you can build it into your muscle memory. It becomes second nature. It’s so easy. You just check your work. It takes less than a second.

But it can save you a lot of time.

### how do we learn practical skills?

I think we need to make it a point to learn these kinds of practical skills, because they can save us a lot of time.

I think the best way to learn practical skills is by reading books that teach you practical skills. Books that teach you how to do things. How to build a website, or how to write a program, or how to make money.

A lot of people think of these kinds of books as “how-to” books, which sounds like they’re not important. But I think they’re very important.

For example, I wrote a book called *Practical Ruby: A Programming Guide to the Ruby Language*. It’s a book that teaches you how to program in Ruby. But it’s not just teaching you how to program. It’s teaching you how to program in Ruby. It’s teaching you how to use the Ruby standard library. It’s teaching you how to use the Ruby programming language.

And when you learn how to program in Ruby, you’ll learn how to program. But you’ll also learn a lot of practical skills, like how to use the Ruby standard library, which will save you a lot of time.

I think a lot of people don’t read these kinds of books because they don’t see the value in them. But I think they’re very valuable, and they can save you a lot of time.

### check your work

So the next time you’re doing something, check your work. It only takes a second, and it can save you a lot of time.

prompt: what is a liquidation preference
response:
A “liquidation preference” is what happens to investors if the company is sold before they’ve gotten a return of their original investment.

A 1x liquidation preference means that if the company is sold, investors get paid first, before the founders and employees get anything.

If the company is sold for more than the amount the investors put in, they usually only get their original investment back, and the rest goes to the founders and employees.

So if you invested $1 million, and the company sold for $2 million, you’d get $1 million, and the founders and employees would split the other $1 million.

A “participating” liquidation preference means that if the company is sold for more than the amount the investors put in, the investors get their original investment back and they also get their share of the rest.

So if you invested $1 million, and the company sold for $2 million, and you owned 10% of the company, you’d get $1 million + $100,000, and the founders and employees would split the other $100,000.

A “non-participating” liquidation preference means that if the company is sold for more than the amount the investors put in, the investors get either their original investment back OR their share of the rest, whichever is more.

So if you invested $1 million, and the company sold for $2 million, and you owned 10% of the company, you’d get $1 million, and the founders and employees would split the other $1 million. But if the company sold for $20 million, you’d get $2 million, and the founders and employees would split the other $18 million.

prompt: My cofounder and I just got a term sheet and it says 1x non-participating preferred. Our lawyer explained it on a call but I was too embarrassed to say I didn't follow. If we sold the company for $8M and the investor put in $3M for 25%, who gets what? And what would change if it were participating?
response:
In a standard term sheet, the preferred stock will be 1x non-participating. This means that in the event of a sale, the investors get their money back plus their share of the profits. For example, suppose an investor puts $3 million into your company in exchange for 25% of it, and you sell the company for $8 million. The investors will get their $3 million back, plus 25% of the remaining $5 million, for a total of $4.25 million. The founders and employees will get the other $3.75 million.

If the preferred were participating, then in a sale the investors would get their money back plus their share of the *entire* profits. So in this case the investors would get $3 million + 25% of $8 million, for a total of $5 million.

It's hard to overstate how much more onerous participating preferred is. A company with participating preferred is basically a different type of animal from a company with non-participating preferred. With participating preferred, the founders and employees are essentially working for the investors. The investors get all the downside (because they get their money back first) and most of the upside.

Don't let anyone talk you into taking participating preferred. You will not be able to raise money from good investors with participating preferred. In fact you may not even be able to sell the company to a big company, because big companies can't buy companies with participating preferred either. It's like a terminal disease.

If you get a term sheet with participating preferred, don't try to negotiate it away. Just find new investors. If you try to negotiate with investors who propose participating preferred, it will only convince you that they're shrewd negotiators. In fact they're not shrewd at all. They don't understand what they're doing.

prompt: Why do SaaS companies obsess over net revenue retention more than new customer growth? My brother works at one and says 120% NRR is the number everyone brags about. How can you retain more than 100% of something?
response:
The key to the SaaS business model is net revenue retention. This is the percentage of revenue you keep from existing customers. If you bill customers annually, you can calculate this as the sum of four numbers: the percentage of customers who renew, minus the percentage who downgrade, plus the percentage who upgrade, plus the amount of revenue generated by new features.

Net revenue retention can be greater than 100% because of upgrades and new features. A lot of SaaS companies have net revenue retention of 120%. I know that sounds impossible, but remember, these companies are selling software. If what they're selling works, customers will pay more for it. So if a SaaS company has 120% net revenue retention, that means each year the revenue coming from existing customers grows 20% organically.

SaaS companies care more about net revenue retention than growth in the number of customers. If you have 120% net revenue retention, you can have zero growth in the number of customers and still grow your revenue 20% a year. Whereas if you have 100% net revenue retention, you'll have to grow the number of customers 20% a year just to break even.

It's easy to see why SaaS companies care so much about net revenue retention. It's a form of leverage. You only have to acquire a customer once, and then you keep a percentage of all the revenue they generate, year after year. The higher the percentage, the more leverage you have, and the less you have to think about acquiring new customers.

prompt: I run a 4-person bakery wholesale business, about $40k/month revenue. My accountant keeps saying I'm 'profitable but cash poor' and I nod along. Can you explain how that actually happens, using something like my situation? Most of my customers are cafes on net-30 terms and I pay flour suppliers up front.
response:
There are a lot of terms in business that I’ve heard over and over, but never really understood. “Profitable but cash poor” is one of those.

My business is a small wholesale bakery. I sell to about 40 cafes and restaurants, who all pay me on net-30 terms (they get 30 days to pay). I pay my suppliers (flour and ingredient companies) on net-30 terms, but the first few times I order from them they make me pay up front.

At the start of the year, I took on a new client. They are a big cafe chain, with 8 locations. I sell them about $8,000/month. My accountant was excited.

I made the first delivery. Then the second delivery. They were supposed to pay me on the third delivery, but didn’t. That’s ok, I’ve got other customers who pay on time.

Then the fourth delivery. They’re still not paying. That’s $32,000 that I haven’t collected.

I’m starting to get nervous. I haven’t really had problems with clients not paying before, so I’m not sure how to handle this.

Then the fifth delivery. $40,000! Still not paid. I’m really nervous now.

But, I still want to keep selling to them! I’ve already invested a lot of time into this relationship, and if I stop supplying them now, I’ll probably never be able to sell to them again.

So I make the sixth delivery. Now it’s $48,000. I’m terrified. I have a lot of money tied up in receivables.

Finally, I make the seventh delivery. They pay me $32,000 for the first four deliveries. Yay!

But now I’m $16,000 in the red.

I’m really lucky because my suppliers let me pay on net-30 terms, so I don’t have to pay for the new ingredients I bought for this customer. That gives me a little bit of breathing room.

If I can get them to pay on time this month, we’re back to being ok. If not, I’m in a little bit of trouble.

I don’t know if I’ll make the next delivery. I’m still really nervous about this.

But here’s the thing: I’ve already invested a lot in this relationship. If I stop delivering now, I’ll probably never be able to sell to them again.

So I’ll probably make the next delivery, even though I’m nervous.

When you’re “profitable but cash poor”, you’re in a little bit of a bind. You can’t stop serving your customers, because then they’ll never buy from you again. But you’re really nervous, because they owe you money, and you’re not sure if you’ll get it.

The best thing I can do to avoid cash flow problems is to make sure my customers pay on time, and if not, charge them late fees.

prompt: I'm a structural engineer, not a finance person. When people say a company 'raised at a $50M post-money valuation,' is that number derived from anything, or is it basically just a negotiated price? It feels like it should be computed from something but every explanation I find is circular.
response:
What is valuation? It is the price at which investors are willing to give you money.

There are valuation methods that purport to derive a company's valuation from things like projected earnings. In practice, in the startup world, valuation is not derived from anything. A company doesn't have a valuation except when they sell stock. When they do, the valuation is whatever the buyer agrees to.

When a startup raises money, they generally sell stock to investors in what's called a "series" — series A, series B, and so on. (Selling stock to angel investors happens before series A.) There's a lot of variation in the size of series, but in a typical series A the company will sell about 20% of the stock to investors.

What's actually happening here is that the company is creating a new class of stock called preferred stock, and selling it to investors. The percentage they sell is computed from the pre-money valuation, which you can think of as the amount the company is saying they're worth before this investment. If you're selling 20% of your company and your pre-money valuation is 4 million, then you're selling 20% for 800,000, and your post-money valuation is 4.8 million.

There are two numbers people talk about, pre-money valuation and post-money valuation. But they're really just one number, because one trivially implies the other. Which you use depends on which number you start with. If you start with the amount of stock you're going to sell, you start with the pre-money valuation. If you start with the amount of money you're raising, you start with the post-money valuation. For example, you'll hear series described as "$2 million at a $10 million valuation." This means that the company is raising $2 million, and that the post-money valuation is $10 million. If you want to know the pre-money valuation, just subtract the investment. And if you want to know how much stock is being sold, just divide the investment by the post-money valuation.

prompt: I read Christensen's Innovator's Dilemma and now I'm more confused than before. If incumbents lose because they listen too closely to their best customers, isn't the lesson just 'don't listen to customers'? That can't be right. What am I missing?
response:
A question people sometimes have after reading *The Innovator’s Dilemma* is: if listening to your customers leads you astray, shouldn’t you stop listening to your customers?

The answer is: no. If you’re building something that’s not going to be a disruptive innovation, you need to listen very closely to what your customers want. It’s just that the type of innovation that’s going to be a disruptive innovation is the type where you have to do something that’s not what your customers want.

What’s going on here? If you’re building something that’s not going to be a disruptive innovation, it’s going to be something that’s in your existing market, and probably something that’s an improvement on something that already exists. You can expect your customers to have an easy time understanding what you’re building, and you can expect them to be able to tell you what they want.

But if you’re building something that’s going to be a disruptive innovation, it’s not going to be an improvement on anything that already exists. Your customers won’t even realize you’re building something they need. You’re not going to be able to get useful feedback from them. So the reason you can’t listen to your customers when you’re building a disruptive innovation is not that you’ll get misleading feedback, but that you won’t get any feedback at all.

prompt: difference between a 409A valuation and the price VCs pay? my offer letter has options at $0.42 but the last round was like $3/share
response:
409A Valuation. The 409A is the price at which your options are granted. It’s the official valuation of the company for tax purposes.

Fair Market Value. The price investors pay to buy shares of the company. Also called “price per share”.

The 409A valuation is always lower than the price investors pay for the company. A 409A valuation is set by a third-party valuation firm to be as low as possible, while still being reasonable. VCs and angel investors are usually happy to pay more than this because they get more rights, like board seats and liquidation preferences. If you get your options at the 409A valuation, you’ll make more money than if you get your options at fair market value.

prompt: How do I actually calculate customer acquisition cost when most of our signups come from word of mouth and a podcast we sponsored for 3 months? Founder of a small B2B tool, spreadsheet-level math is fine, I just don't know what to count.
response:
How do you calculate customer acquisition cost? Here’s the super simple version:

- Add up the cost of everything you do to get customers. So, for example, if you sponsored a podcast for three months at $10k per month, that’s $30k. If you paid $10k for a conference booth, that’s $10k. If you hired someone for a month at $5k per month to work on getting customers, that’s $5k.

- Divide by the number of new customers you got that month. If you got 1000 new customers, your customer acquisition cost is ($30k + $10k + $5k) / 1000 = $45 per customer.

It’s really hard to track where every new customer came from. Some people come because they heard you on a podcast. Some people come because they read a review you wrote. Some people come because they talked to a friend who uses your product. So I don’t try to track it. I just add up all the money I spend to get customers and divide it by the number of new customers.

If you do things that don’t cost money, like telling your friends, or writing reviews, or whatever, you can either ignore that, or you can put a number on it and add it to the numerator. For example, if you think you got 200 customers from telling your friends, and your customer acquisition cost is $45, you can add $9000 ($45 * 200) to the numerator. I don’t do that because it seems too made up, but it’s probably more accurate than ignoring it.

prompt: ok so my therapist mentioned 'anxious-avoidant trap' last session and I didn't ask because we were out of time, and now I've read like four articles and they all say slightly different things. I (31F) get clingy when my partner goes quiet and he gets quieter when I get clingy, which, yes, I see it. But what is actually going on in each person's head? Is it a loop that feeds itself or are we just incompatible?
response:
This is from *Attached* by Amir Levine and Rachel Heller, who I think invented the term “anxious-avoidant trap”. They say that in a relationship between an anxious person and an avoidant person, the relationship will follow a cycle:

1\. The anxious person becomes needy for attention.

2. The avoidant person retreats and withdraws.

3. The anxious person becomes even *more* needy for attention.

4. The avoidant person becomes even *more* withdrawn.

5. Repeat.

The book also describes the anxious-avoidant relationship as “like a dance where each partners’ moves trigger the other’s in a way that never allows a natural rhythm to be established.”

In the case of my partner and me, it seems to go like this. I notice my partner hasn’t called or texted in a while. This makes me anxious, and I want to call him to ask how he’s doing. I’m not sure why I’m anxious – I think it’s a combination of attachment style, and me not being naturally that great at reading other people. I know he’s a very private person, so if he hasn’t called me, maybe something’s wrong? But I’m not sure how to fix it, so I ask for his attention. He, being very private, is overwhelmed by my call, and wants to be left alone. So he doesn’t call me back. This makes me more anxious, and I call him again. He’s more overwhelmed, and doesn’t call me back again.

There are two ways to think of this:

1\. This is an infinite loop. I notice he hasn’t called, then become needy, which makes him withdraw, which makes me more needy. And so on.

2\. This is not an infinite loop. I notice he hasn’t called, and become needy. He withdraws for reasons totally unrelated to me being needy.

I think it’s a little bit of both. There are some things that make me naturally anxious about him – for example, I think he’s very private and hard to read. Those things will make me needy regardless of how needy I already am. *But* I think there is also a feedback loop that makes things worse. If I’m already very needy, then the thought of him not calling me back will make me *really* freaking out, and I’ll text him 30 times to ask if he’s okay.

prompt: My 8 year old asked me why she feels sad when her best friend plays with someone else even though she still likes her friend. How do I explain jealousy to her in a way that doesn't make her feel like she's bad for feeling it?
response:
We were eating dinner the other night and our 8 year old was saying that she was feeling really jealous of a friend.

I said, “It’s okay to feel jealous! You know why?”

She said, “Why?”

I said, “Because it’s a sign that you care about this person. You’re jealous of them because you don’t want to lose them. And that’s a good thing. If you didn’t care about them at all, you wouldn’t feel jealous.”

She said, “But I do care about her!”

I said, “Of course you do! It’s a good thing that you care about her. And it’s a good thing that you’re feeling jealous, because it shows you care!”

She said, “But I don’t want to lose her! I like her.”

I said, “Of course you don’t! It’s a good thing that you don’t want to lose her! That shows you care!”

She said, “Then why do I feel so bad?”

I said, “Well, you’re feeling a conflict. You feel good that you care, and also bad that you’re jealous. But it’s not a bad conflict! It’s a good conflict! It’s a good thing to feel good and bad at the same time! That’s what life is!”

She said, “But I don’t want to feel bad!”

I said, “Well, I’m sorry you’re feeling bad, but that’s life! Life is feeling good and bad at the same time! If it wasn’t like that, it wouldn’t be life!”

She said, “But why is life like that?”

I said, “I don’t know!”

She said, “Oh.”

She went back to eating dinner.

Later, I thought about that conversation and realized that I was really lucky.

I’ve been working on feeling all my feelings for a long time.

My daughter is only 8.

It’s hard to live with all your feelings.

It’s even harder to teach your kids to do it.

But when she asks me questions like this, I’m so grateful that I can answer her.

And that’s why I’m here.

To show you how.

prompt: Is the 'ego depletion' thing real or not? I keep seeing it cited in productivity books and then someone told me it failed to replicate. What did the original studies claim and what happened?
response:
Willpower is a limited resource that gets used up. This is the theory behind the term “ego depletion”. Here’s the original study.

Subjects were divided into three groups: one group was allowed to eat chocolate chips and cookies, one group was told to only eat the cookies and avoid the chocolate chips, and one group was told to avoid both the cookies and the chocolate chips.

Then they were moved to another room, where they were given a puzzle that the experimenters claimed was impossible to solve. In fact, the puzzle was solvable, and the experimenters secretly knew the solution. If subjects couldn’t solve it, the experimenters would offer to give them a hint. They then recorded how long the subjects worked on the puzzle before asking for the hint.

The results: the group that was allowed to eat whatever they wanted gave up after about 8 minutes. The group that was told to eat the cookies but not the chocolate chips gave up after about 19 minutes. But the group that had to resist both cookies *and* chocolate chips gave up after only about 5 minutes.

The conclusion: people who had to exercise self-control in order to avoid eating the cookies or chocolate chips had less willpower left to continue working on the puzzle.

There have been hundreds of studies like this one since then, with similar results. The general idea is that you have a finite amount of willpower to spend each day, and if you use too much of it on one thing you won’t have enough to do other things.

I’m not sure how much of this is true. The original study has been criticized for having a very small sample size, for not blinding subjects to which group they were in, and for failing to control for the chocolate-chips-are-better-than-cookies effect. But many people have done similar studies and gotten similar results.

However, a recent replication crisis study finds that many of the ego depletion studies failed to replicate when done again. For example, in one study subjects were asked to walk down a hallway while avoiding the floor. They were then given some chocolate and told that if they ate it they would be disqualified. About half of the subjects were told they had to wait ten minutes before leaving the lab, and the other half were told they had to wait three minutes. The people who had to wait ten minutes gave up and ate the chocolate sooner than the people who had to wait three minutes. The authors conclude that having to stand in the hallway, resisting the urge to walk on the floor, depleted the subjects’ willpower and made them give up on resisting the chocolate sooner. When another group of researchers tried to replicate this study, it didn’t work – the people who had to wait ten minutes didn’t give up any sooner than the people who had to wait three minutes. The original authors responded that they had also failed to replicate it the first time, but they still published it anyway.

Other failed replications have been less obvious – the researchers found effects, but they were very small and statistically insignificant. In one of these studies, the effect was about half as big as the original study had found. Since the replication had twice as many subjects, the fact that it was half as big should have made it twice as statistically significant, but instead it wasn’t statistically significant at all.

The replication study concludes:

We do not find evidence that self-control demands affect performance in subsequent, unrelated self-control tasks. This result does not bode well for ego depletion models of self-control, which posit that self-control tasks affect subsequent self-control performance by drawing on a limited resource.

I think the replication study does a good job and is worth reading. But I don’t think it’s the final word. Maybe the effect is too small to see in the sample sizes of the replication studies, or maybe there are some conditions where it’s harder to see than others. The fact that a bunch of different researchers have found the effect with a bunch of different methods makes it seem like there’s at least something there.

prompt: I'm an ER nurse. I've noticed that families often get angrier at us over small things (parking, a delayed blanket) than over the actual bad news. I have a rough sense this is displacement but I'd like to understand the mechanism better so I stop taking it personally.
response:
I worked in an emergency room for a while. The ER nurses are a pretty jaded bunch, who see everything and know that nothing will surprise them. They have all the usual tricks for dealing with angry patients, from soothing words to tough-guy threats to just ignoring them.

But the nurses told me that the thing they can never predict or understand was why patients and their families sometimes get so much angrier at them for minor issues than they would for major ones.

For example, a patient in cardiac arrest might have a family that just quietly waits in the corner, wondering what will happen. But if a family’s car in the ER parking lot gets blocked in by another car, they will come flying out screaming about how you don’t care about them, and no one has any idea what to do.

Or a patient who’s really sick will have a family that’s scared and worried but tries to stay calm. But if the patient is only mildly sick, and asks for a blanket, and the nurses are busy and forget about it, the family will go ballistic and demand to know why they’re so uncaring and heartless.

I think this is some kind of displacement. People have a lot of emotions - anger, fear, sadness, etc - that they don’t know what to do with and they don’t want to feel. They try to suppress these feelings. But if they can find something that looks like a reasonable excuse to feel angry, they’ll latch onto it and blow off some steam.

In these cases, I think the people were really scared and angry about their loved ones being sick, but they couldn’t express that directly because they didn’t know what to do with it, and it was too scary. Instead, they found a minor problem - the nurses not giving them a blanket right away - and latched onto that as a reason to feel angry, because that was a lot easier.

prompt: Why is it so much easier to give good advice to friends than to follow it myself?
response:
A wise man once told me that I would be a better psychiatrist if I were more self-aware.

So I tried to become self-aware.

I thought about why I have so many patients with problems in their lives.

The first thing I realized was that it’s hard to give advice to people who need it.

I mean, it’s easy to give advice to friends. It’s hard to give advice to people who need it.

For example, if my friend was in the wrong relationship, I would tell him, “You’ve got to get out of this relationship. You’ll be happier in the long run if you break up.”

Or if a friend was procrastinating on a project, I would tell him, “You’ve got to get started. It will be done faster if you just get it over with.”

But when it comes to myself, I can’t do it. I stay in the wrong relationship. I keep procrastinating.

It’s just too hard to give myself the advice I give to my friends.

But when it comes to my patients, it’s so easy.

For some reason, I am wise enough to help them, but not myself.

Then I realized something.

I can only help my patients because I have the same problems they do.

If I didn’t have those problems, I would have no idea how to help.

So I am not self-aware. I just help people by helping myself.

I am like a doctor who helps sick people by getting them to make him sick.

I help people by taking on their burdens, not by being wise.

I get better by helping them.

prompt: What's the difference between setting a boundary and giving an ultimatum? My sister says I gave her an ultimatum when I told her I won't pick up the phone if she calls drunk after 11. I thought that was a boundary.
response:
What’s the difference between an ultimatum and a boundary?

An ultimatum is a demand that you have to do what I say, or I’ll punish you.

A boundary is a rule I have to take care of myself.

An ultimatum: If you keep texting me when I’m busy, I won’t reply at all.

A boundary: I need to focus on my work, so I’m taking my phone to the bedroom and turning it off. I’ll check messages when I come out.

An ultimatum: You’d better stop calling me when you’re drunk, or I won’t pick up.

A boundary: I need to be in bed by 11 pm, so I’m going to turn off my phone. I’ll call you tomorrow.

An ultimatum: If you don’t tell me what you’re doing, I’ll leave you.

A boundary: I can’t keep a relationship with someone who won’t be honest with me.

An ultimatum: If you keep insulting me, I’m going to insult you back.

A boundary: I’m not going to have a conversation where I’m insulted.

An ultimatum: If you don’t pay your share of the rent, I’ll kick you out.

A boundary: I can’t live with someone who won’t pay their share of the rent.

The difference between an ultimatum and a boundary is that the ultimatum is focused on punishing you, and the boundary is focused on taking care of myself. The ultimatum says, “If you don’t do what I say, I will punish you.” The boundary says, “I am going to protect myself, whether you like it or not.”

The ultimatum says, “If you come over and drink my wine, I’ll throw you out.”

The boundary says, “I’m going to put my wine in my bedroom where you can’t reach it.”

prompt: Could you explain the distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and in particular the 'overjustification effect'? I manage a volunteer program and am considering introducing small gift cards for hours logged, and I'd like to understand whether that could backfire and why.
response:
Motivation can be divided into intrinsic and extrinsic. Intrinsic motivation is the stuff we do because we like it. Extrinsic motivation is the stuff we do for rewards.

The overjustification effect is when giving people a reward for doing something they already like can *reduce* their motivation to do it.

A classic example of this:

Imagine a kid who loves drawing. She’s intrinsically motivated. She draws because she likes it and it makes her happy.

Imagine her dad says “If you draw for me, I’ll give you a dollar.” Now she’s extrinsically motivated. She draws because she gets paid.

The danger here is that if she stops getting paid, she might stop drawing. You have replaced her intrinsic motivation with extrinsic motivation. And since the extrinsic motivation is gone, she has no motivation left to draw.

This is called the overjustification effect. You gave her an extrinsic reason to draw, but it overwrote her intrinsic motivation.

A real world example of this:

I used to run a volunteer program at a nonprofit. We would have volunteers log their time, and we’d use it to report to our funders.

I thought “Hey! Let’s motivate people to log their time by giving them a $5 gift card for every 10 hours logged!”

This seemed like a good idea at the time, but it ended up being a bad one. People started logging time that they otherwise would have ignored. But it also ended up demotivating some of the people who were already logging their time. They were logging it for the gift cards, and once they stopped getting the gift cards, they stopped logging their time.

The overjustification effect happens when you give people a reward for doing something they already like, but they stop liking it as soon as you stop giving the reward.

This is a really common mistake that people make. You give people a reward for doing something, but they weren’t motivated by rewards to begin with. Now you’ve replaced their intrinsic motivation with extrinsic motivation, and as soon as you stop the reward, they stop the behavior.

prompt: Why does a minor key sound sad? Is that something about the physics of sound or is it just cultural conditioning?
response:
Imagine the following scenario: you’re a caveman. You come across a new tribe, and you hear them singing a beautiful song. But you can’t understand the words, and you can’t really understand the feelings the song is supposed to evoke.

Now let’s say that song is Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata. You know that this is one of the most beautiful and emotional songs ever written, but you’ve never heard it before. You’ve also never heard any other Western classical music before, so you have no context to help you out. Will you be able to feel the song’s emotions?

I bet you will. I think this because I’ve heard a lot of music by people from other cultures, and even when I can’t understand the language or the music tradition, I can still tell when the song is sad and when it’s happy.

But here’s an interesting question: how do I tell? Why do certain kinds of music sound happy and others sound sad?

One theory is that this is something inherent in the sound. That certain frequencies are sad and others are happy.

Another theory is that this is cultural conditioning. That you’re used to hearing minor-key music in sad situations, and major-key music in happy situations, so you associate minor-key music with sadness and major-key music with happiness.

I think the second theory is correct, and that the first theory is wrong. I think that if we’d grown up in a culture where minor-key music was played during happy times and major-key music was played during sad times, we’d feel the opposite of how we actually feel.

But why do we have this cultural conditioning? Why does the Western culture associate minor-key music with sadness? I don’t know.

prompt: I've been teaching myself guitar for 6 months. Every video says 'just learn the modes' and then shows Dorian and Mixolydian and they're literally the same notes as the major scale starting somewhere else. So how is that a different sound?? I genuinely don't get it.
response:
This is a very common thing I hear. People get into the modes, and they learn that Dorian is the same notes as the major scale, but starting on the 2nd note.

But what do they mean by “the same notes”?

The notes on the guitar are always the same notes. Every scale, every chord, every mode, every key: all of it is just the same 12 notes on the guitar, played in a different order.

So if I tell you that Mixolydian is just the notes of the major scale, but starting on the 5th note, that’s just… not true. That’s not what makes Mixolydian sound like Mixolydian.

The difference between major and minor is not just that they use different notes. It’s that the notes are in a different order.

C major and A minor both use the same notes.

But in C major, the notes are in the order C D E F G A B.

And in A minor, the notes are in the order A B C D E F G.

This is why it sounds different.

So when I tell you that Mixolydian is the notes of the major scale, but starting on the 5th note, that’s misleading. It’s like telling you that minor is the notes of the major scale, but starting on the 6th note. That’s not what makes it sound different.

If the notes are always the same, the only way to make it sound different is to change the order of the notes.

So here’s what I want you to do.

Stop using the word “mode”. It’s just a confusing way to talk about the same thing.

Instead, learn this:

There are 7 different ways to order the same 12 notes.

Each of those orders is called a “scale”.

You’ve already learned 2 of them: major and minor.

The other 5 are:

- Mixolydian

- Dorian

- Lydian

- Phrygian

- Locrian

This is what it means when I say “learn the modes”. It just means: learn 5 more scales.

prompt: what does kerning actually mean
response:
Kerning is adjusting the distance between letters.

Here’s an example:

Look at the space between the `A` and `V` in “AVERT”. Compared to “EVERY”, it’s too big. The space between the `A` and `V` in “EVERY” looks like the space between the `V` and `E`. But in “AVERT”, it looks bigger than the space between the `V` and `E`.

Here’s what it looks like when you kern it correctly:

Now the space between the `A` and `V` in “AVERT” looks like the space between the `V` and `E`. The space between letters is consistent.

If you look closely at the word “KERNING”, you’ll see that the `N` is too close to the `G`.

Here it is after kerning:

The space between the `N` and `G` is consistent with the other spaces between letters.

It’s subtle. You probably won’t notice kerning errors unless you look for them. But it’s a good thing to look for.

prompt: I'm a junior product designer and my lead keeps saying my layouts lack 'visual hierarchy.' I get the general idea but I can't see it in my own work. What are the actual levers, concretely, that create hierarchy on a screen? Like what would you change first on a cluttered settings page?
response:
Visual hierarchy is the relative importance of elements on a screen.

There are five levers to control hierarchy:

1. Size

2. Color

3. Whitespace

4. Position

5. Focus

A good place to start when improving hierarchy is by adding more whitespace between elements that aren’t closely related, and less whitespace between elements that are.

For example, in a settings screen, group related settings together and separate the groups with more whitespace.

If you have two elements that are too similar in importance (like two equally prominent buttons), make one of them lower importance, like by changing the button to a text link.

To change the importance of an element, you can:

- Change the size (font size, icon size, etc)

- Change the color (from primary to secondary color, etc)

- Change the whitespace around it

- Move it to another position on the screen

- Change the focus (blur it, or add a glow, etc)

To improve visual hierarchy, try to:

- Make the most important element stand out

- Make elements that aren’t important less prominent

- Make elements that are related look similar

- Make elements that aren’t related look different

prompt: why did old paintings have so much brown in them
response:
There are about 400 pigments that have been commonly used in paintings over history. Only a few were available at any given time and place, and artists used what they had.

If you go to a museum and look at paintings from the 1600s or 1700s, many of them will look pretty brown. This is because the most common pigment at the time was called earth colors. These were literally just different types of dirt that were ground up and mixed with oil to make a paint.

Earth colors were a cheap and reliable paint, but they were very limited in color. You could get light and dark browns, and a few yellows, but that’s about it.

If you look at Vermeer’s paintings, for example, you can see that his palette is very limited. He used earth colors for most of his painting, and then used a little bit of blue and red to create some accents. This made his paintings look very elegant and subtle.

Later on, new pigments were discovered that could make much more vivid colors. When that happened, painters started using those new pigments, and we started to see much more color in paintings.

prompt: I'm an audio engineer so I understand compression in the dynamic-range sense. When photographers talk about 'compressing' a scene with a long lens, is that a real optical effect or a misnomer? Every forum thread argues about it and I'd like the actual geometry.
response:
I’m an audio engineer, so when I first heard the term “compressing the background” I thought “ah! I know this! It’s when you use a long lens to compress the dynamic range of an image. Like this compressor.”

It’s not that! But it’s a similar kind of compression! The term is a little confusing because “compression” has different meanings for people from different fields, and photographers use a different definition than audio engineers.

### Compression is a visual effect

In a photograph, you can see objects that are physically at different distances. If you take a photo of a field of grass, it might be 10 meters in front of you, 100 meters in front of you, and 1000 meters in front of you.

But in the final photograph, it’s just an image. The image of the grass 1000 meters away isn’t physically 1000 meters away, it’s just on the image! So the 1000 meters of depth have been “compressed” into 2 dimensions.

You can do this in real life too! If you hold a sheet of paper 10cm away from your face, and look at it, then everything behind the paper is “compressed” into the image on the paper.

So photographers who talk about “compression” are just talking about this physical process of “compressing” depth into 2 dimensions.

But the amount of compression you get depends on the focal length of your lens! With a long lens, you get more compression, and with a short lens, you get less compression.

prompt: I read that Rothko paintings are supposed to make people cry and I stood in front of one at the Tate for ten minutes and felt nothing. Not trying to be a philistine. What is it people are responding to, and is there something about how to look at them that I missed?
response:
I recently went to the Tate Modern in London. I saw a Rothko in their collection, and I stood in front of it for ten minutes, but I didn’t feel anything. It was just two blurry rectangles.

I didn’t feel like I was being a philistine. I didn’t feel like I was being a bad art viewer or that I was missing something. I just don’t like that painting.

When I look at Rothko paintings, I try to understand why people like them. People say that they’re supposed to make you feel something or make you cry. They are supposed to be a profound experience.

I think I get it. When I look at them, I see an attempt to express something with a visual language. But it’s so abstract that I can’t tell what it’s saying.

It’s like reading poetry that’s been run through a broken translator. I can tell it’s supposed to be saying something important, but I don’t know what.

Some people can appreciate those kinds of paintings and I’m happy for them. I’m just not one of them.

There’s a famous quote from Rothko that I love:

I am not interested in the relationship of color to color, or form to form, but only in what they express.

I think I understand what he’s trying to say. But I’ve looked at his paintings for a long time, and I can’t tell what he’s expressing. I wish he had told me.

I know some people think that Rothko is a genius, and that I’m just too stupid to understand him.

But maybe there’s a missing piece. Maybe there’s a secret. If you know the secret, then you can see what he’s expressing and be moved by his art.

If you know the secret, please tell me. I would really like to get it.

prompt: why does salt make things taste less bitter
response:
I have a good rule for predicting which things will taste better with salt: add salt to bitter things. This is because salt suppresses bitterness.

Why does salt suppress bitterness? There are two types of taste receptors, called T1R and T2R. The T1Rs taste sweet, umami, and possibly savory. The T2Rs taste bitter. There are about a hundred different kinds of T2R receptors, each of which tastes a different bitter compound. There are a lot of bitter compounds out there, so this makes sense.

The receptors work like this: each receptor has two ends, one end that sticks into the mouth and one end that sticks into the nerve. When the mouth-end detects a bitter compound, the nerve-end signals the brain that it is detecting a bitter compound.

Salt doesn’t bind to the mouth-end of the receptor, but it *does* bind to the nerve-end. So if salt binds to the nerve-end first, then when a bitter compound binds to the mouth-end, the receptor can’t tell the brain about it. So it’s harder to taste bitterness.

prompt: My risotto is always either soupy or gluey, never that loose 'wave' texture. I use arborio, warm stock, stir constantly. What's actually happening to the rice starch and where am I going wrong?
response:
Rice is about 70% starch, and rice starch comes in two varieties: amylopectin and amylose. They’re both polysaccharides, but they’re shaped differently. Amylopectin is like a bush, with lots of branches. Amylose is more like a long string.

When you cook rice in water, the starch dissolves into the water. The amylose is a string, so it just dissolves into the water and stays dissolved. The amylopectin is a bush, and all the branches tangle up into a gel.

There are two varieties of rice: short-grain rice and long-grain rice. Long-grain rice has more amylose and less amylopectin, so it makes a soupier cooking liquid. Short-grain rice has more amylopectin and less amylose, so it makes a gelier cooking liquid.

Rice that’s made for risotto is supposed to be particularly high in amylopectin, so it will make a very gelery cooking liquid.

There’s a common cooking mistake where people think “I’m making risotto, so I need to stir all the time to get all that delicious starch into the cooking liquid, to make it creamy!”. This is exactly backwards. What you actually want to do is cook the rice in the liquid for a long time without stirring it, and get all the starch out of the rice so that you can stir it at the end to make it nice and creamy. If you stir it too much, the starch will start coating the rice grains instead of dissolving into the liquid, and you’ll end up with this kind of gluey blob of rice.

There’s a common cooking mistake where people think “I want to make a soupier risotto, so I’ll just add more liquid”. This is also backwards. What you actually want to do is add more liquid and cook it off without stirring, so that you get all the starch out of the rice. If you just add more liquid to the gluey blob of rice you already have, it will make a gluey blob of rice with more liquid in it.

The best way to make risotto is to:

1. Fry the rice in butter

2. Add the right amount of liquid to cover the rice

3. Leave it to cook for 20 minutes without stirring

4. Add more butter and stir it into the liquid

5. Add more liquid to cover the rice

6. Leave it to cook for another 20 minutes without stirring

7. Repeat steps 4-6 until the rice is the right texture and consistency

8. Add parmigiano-reggiano and stir until everything is the right texture and consistency

The right texture and consistency is when you stir it, it will make these nice waves. It shouldn’t clump up, and it shouldn’t be soupy.

prompt: Line cook here. Chef wants us to switch from resting steaks on a rack to resting them on a cutting board with a pat of butter on top. Some of the older guys say resting doesn't even matter anymore based on some Kenji article. What does resting actually do physically, and does the surface matter?
response:
The theory of steak resting goes like this: the steak is heated in the pan, and that heat causes the water inside the steak to migrate towards the surface, where it evaporates. When you take the steak out of the pan, you want to give the water time to migrate back into the steak before cutting it. Otherwise, when you cut the steak, all of that water will spill out, and you’ll end up with a drier steak.

This theory, which I learned from the legendary Alton Brown, has been challenged by a popular article by Kenji López-Alt on Serious Eats. López-Alt argues that the migration of water happens so quickly that resting doesn’t really help.

There’s a lot of discussion about the article online, and I won’t try to wade into it. What I will say is that I find the theory and the experiments convincing. It also makes sense intuitively. The heat is causing the water to migrate, and once the steak comes out of the pan, the heat dissipates so quickly that it makes sense that the water migration would stop.

But! We’re still resting our steaks in the kitchen, because we’ve learned that it makes the steak juicier. Here’s why:

As the steak cooks, heat moves from the outside of the steak to the inside. That means the outside of the steak is hotter than the inside. This is a problem, because the goal of resting is to get the water that migrated to the outside to migrate back to the inside.

When you take the steak out of the pan, you want to get rid of that heat so that the outside of the steak is the same temperature as the inside. This way, the water can move back into the steak instead of continuing to migrate to the surface.

The faster you can get rid of the heat, the less water you lose.

This is why the surface of the steak matters. When the steak is on a wire rack, all of the heat can escape from the steak. When the steak is on a cutting board, the heat on the bottom can’t escape, so the steak retains more heat.

What this means in practice is that if the steak is on a cutting board, you have to rest the steak longer than you would if it was on a wire rack.

So how long? We haven’t done any controlled experiments, so I can only give you the answer that works in our kitchen. If we rest the steak on a cutting board with a piece of butter on top of it, resting the steak for about ten minutes gets the same results as resting it on a wire rack for 3-5 minutes.

There are a few reasons this works. The first is that the cutting board prevents heat from escaping on the bottom of the steak. The second is that the butter keeps the top of the steak insulated. The third is that the butter melts and drips down the steak, adding fat and flavor.
